Could you walk me through it step by step? Let \( n \ge 3 \) be an integer. Two players, Ana and Beto, play the following game. Ana tags the vertices of a regular \( n \)-gon with the numbers from 1 to \( n \), in any order she wants. Every vertex must be tagged with a different number. Then, we place a turkey in each of the \( n \) vertices. If Beto whistles, each turkey moves to the adjacent vertex with the greater tag. If Beto claps, each turkey moves to the adjacent vertex with the lower tag. Beto wins if, after some number of whistles and claps, he gets to move all the turkeys to the same vertex. Ana wins if she can tag the vertices so that Beto can't do this. For each \( n \ge 3 \), determine which player has a winning strategy.

A concise solution goes like this: **The game**

For a fixed labelling of the vertices let  

* \(W\) be the map “whistle’’ : a turkey at a vertex goes to the
adjacent vertex whose tag is **larger** (if the two neighbours have
different tags the larger one is unique; if they are equal the choice
does not matter – the argument below works for any deterministic choice),

* \(C\) be the map “clap’’ : a turkey goes to the adjacent vertex whose
tag is **smaller**.

Thus after a word \(a_{1}a_{2}\dots a_{k}\;(a_{i}\in\{W,C\})\) the set of
vertices occupied by the turkeys is  

\[
a_{k}\bigl(a_{k-1}(\dots a_{1}(V)\dots )\bigr),\qquad V=\{1,\dots ,n\}.
\]

Beto wins iff there is a word that sends the whole set \(V\) to a
singleton; such a word is called a **reset word** for the
deterministic automaton \((V,\{W,C\})\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 1.  Even \(n\) – Ana can prevent a reset word  

Assume that \(n\) is even and Ana writes the numbers clockwise in the
natural order  

\[
1,2,3,\dots ,n .
\]

For a vertex \(i\;(1\le i\le n)\) let the neighbours be \(i-1\) and
\(i+1\) (indices are taken modulo \(n\)).  
Because the numbers increase clockwise, the neighbour with the larger
label is the clockwise neighbour, except for the vertex \(n\) whose
larger neighbour is \(n-1\).  Consequently

\[
W(i)=\begin{cases}
i+1 & (i\neq n),\\[2pt]
n-1 & (i=n),
\end{cases}\qquad
C(i)=\begin{cases}
i-1 & (i\neq 1),\\[2pt]
2   & (i=1).
\end{cases}
\]

In both cases the image of a vertex has opposite parity to the vertex
itself.  Hence

* \(W\) sends every odd vertex to an even vertex and every even vertex
to an odd one;
* the same holds for \(C\).

The initial set of occupied vertices is \(V=\{1,\dots ,n\}\); it
contains both parities.  After any single move (whistle or clap) the
set of occupied vertices still contains **both** parities, because each
parity is mapped onto the other one.  By induction the same is true
after any finite sequence of moves.  Therefore the set of occupied
vertices can never become a singleton.

Thus for every even \(n\) Ana has a winning strategy (the monotone
labelling above).

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 2.  Odd \(n\) – Beto can always reset  

Now let \(n\) be odd and keep an arbitrary labelling of the vertices.
Denote by  

\[
W(v)=\text{the neighbour of }v\text{ with the larger tag},\qquad
C(v)=\text{the neighbour of }v\text{ with the smaller tag}.
\]

For a set \(S\subseteq V\) write  

\[
W(S)=\{W(v):v\in S\},\qquad C(S)=\{C(v):v\in S\}.
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### Lemma 1  
For every non‑empty set \(S\subseteq V\) with \(|S|>1\) one of the two
sets \(W(S),C(S)\) is **strictly smaller** than \(S\).

*Proof.*  
Consider the directed edges \(\{v\to W(v)\mid v\in S\}\).  They are
\( |S| \) edges whose heads lie in \(W(S)\).  Because the underlying
graph is a simple cycle, each vertex can be the head of at most two
such edges (its two incident edges).  Hence  

\[
|S|\le 2|W(S)|.
\tag{1}
\]

The same reasoning gives  

\[
|S|\le 2|C(S)|.
\tag{2}
\]

If both inequalities were equalities, then every vertex of \(W(S)\)
(and of \(C(S)\)) would have indegree exactly two, which would force the
cycle to be oriented consistently around the whole polygon.  That can
happen only when \(n\) is even (the orientation would then alternate
odd/even).  Since \(n\) is odd, at least one of the two inequalities is
strict, i.e. either \(|W(S)|<|S|\) or \(|C(S)|<|S|\). ∎



--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### Lemma 2  
Starting from the whole set \(V\) Beto can reach a singleton after at
most \(n-1\) moves.

*Proof.*  
Apply Lemma 1 repeatedly.  As long as the current set contains more than
one vertex, Beto chooses the letter (whistle or clap) that strictly
decreases its size.  Each move reduces the cardinality, so after at most
\(|V|-1=n-1\) moves a set of size 1 is obtained. ∎



--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### Winning strategy for Beto  

Beto proceeds as follows.

1. **While** more than one vertex is occupied,  
   *look at the current set \(S\) of occupied vertices;*  
   by Lemma 1 either \(W(S)\) or \(C(S)\) is smaller.  
   He whistles if \(|W(S)|<|S|\) and claps otherwise.

2. The process stops exactly when all turkeys stand on the same vertex.

Because Lemma 2 guarantees that the size of the occupied set decreases
at every step, the algorithm terminates after finitely many moves.
Hence for every odd \(n\) Beto has a winning strategy, independent of
Ana’s initial labelling.

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 3.  Conclusion  

* **If \(n\) is even**, Ana can label the vertices in increasing order
clockwise; then every move swaps the parity of the occupied vertices,
so the set of occupied vertices always contains both parities and can
never shrink to a single vertex.  Ana wins.

* **If \(n\) is odd**, for any labelling Beto can repeatedly apply the
letter (whistle or clap) that strictly reduces the number of distinct
occupied vertices; this is always possible by Lemma 1, and after at most
\(n-1\) steps all turkeys occupy one vertex.  Beto wins.

\[
\boxed{\text{Beto wins for odd }n,\qquad
       \text{Ana wins for even }n.}
\]

Where should I start to avoid common pitfalls? Gold dust which is not panned contains $k\%$ of pure gold. After each panning, $p\%$ of the impurities are washed off and $q\%$ of gold are lost. How many pannings must be carried out for the percentage of pure gold in the gold dust to be not less than $r$?

Sure, let's start with the idea: **Let us denote**

* the initial proportion of gold in the dust  

\[
a=\frac{k}{100},\qquad\text{so the impurity proportion is }b=1-a=\frac{100-k}{100}.
\]

* the fraction of gold that **remains** after one panning  

\[
\alpha =1-\frac{q}{100},
\]

* the fraction of impurity that **remains** after one panning  

\[
\beta =1-\frac{p}{100}.
\]

(Thus \(p\%\) of the impurity is removed, i.e. only \(\beta\) of it stays, and \(q\%\) of the gold is lost, i.e. only \(\alpha\) of it stays.)

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 1.  Gold‑percentage after \(n\) pannings  

After \(n\) repetitions

\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{gold mass }&=a\,\alpha^{\,n},\\[2mm]
\text{impurity mass }&=b\,\beta^{\,n},\\[2mm]
\text{total mass }&=a\,\alpha^{\,n}+b\,\beta^{\,n}.
\end{aligned}
\]

Hence the percentage of gold after \(n\) pannings is  

\[
G_n=\frac{a\,\alpha^{\,n}}{a\,\alpha^{\,n}+b\,\beta^{\,n}}\times 100 .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 2.  Requirement \(G_n\ge r\)

\[
\frac{a\,\alpha^{\,n}}{a\,\alpha^{\,n}+b\,\beta^{\,n}}\ge\frac{r}{100}
\Longleftrightarrow
a\,\alpha^{\,n}\ge\frac{r}{100}\bigl(a\,\alpha^{\,n}+b\,\beta^{\,n}\bigr).
\]

Multiplying by \(100\) and using \(a=k/100,\;b=(100-k)/100\) gives  

\[
k\,\alpha^{\,n}\ge r\Bigl(\frac{k}{100}\alpha^{\,n}+\frac{100-k}{100}\beta^{\,n}\Bigr)
\Longleftrightarrow
\alpha^{\,n}\,k\Bigl(1-\frac{r}{100}\Bigr)\ge
\beta^{\,n}\,\frac{r(100-k)}{100}.
\]

Re‑arranging,

\[
\Bigl(\frac{\alpha}{\beta}\Bigr)^{\!n}\ge
\frac{r(100-k)}{k(100-r)} .
\tag{1}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 3.  Solving for the smallest integer \(n\)

*If the initial dust already satisfies the requirement* (\(k\ge r\)), then no panning is needed:

\[
\boxed{\,n=0\; \text{if }k\ge r\,}.
\]

Otherwise (\(k<r\)) we must solve (1).

Define  

\[
\lambda=\frac{\alpha}{\beta}
      =\frac{1-\dfrac{q}{100}}{\,1-\dfrac{p}{100}\,}.
\]

* **If \(\lambda>1\)** (i.e. the impurity is removed faster than gold is lost, \(p>q\)), the left‑hand side of (1) grows with \(n\) and a finite solution exists.  
  Taking natural logarithms,

  \[
  n\ge
  \frac{\displaystyle\ln\!\Bigl(\dfrac{r(100-k)}{k(100-r)}\Bigr)}
       {\displaystyle\ln(\lambda)} .
  \]

  The smallest integer satisfying the inequality is  

  \[
  \boxed{\;
  n=\Bigl\lceil
  \frac{\ln\!\bigl(\dfrac{r(100-k)}{k(100-r)}\bigr)}
       {\ln\!\bigl(\dfrac{1-q/100}{1-p/100}\bigr)}
  \Bigr\rceil\;},
  \qquad\text{provided }p>q\text{ and }k<r .
  \]

* **If \(\lambda=1\)** (i.e. \(p=q\)), the gold‑percentage never changes; it stays at the initial value \(k\%\).  
  Hence a target \(r>k\) is impossible:

  \[
  \boxed{\text{No finite number of pannings can reach }r\% \;(p=q,\;k<r).}
  \]

* **If \(\lambda<1\)** (i.e. \(p<q\)), the impurity is removed more slowly than gold is lost, so the gold‑percentage actually **decreases** with each panning. Again a target \(r>k\) cannot be reached:

  \[
  \boxed{\text{Impossible when }p<q\text{ and }k<r.}
  \]

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 4.  Final answer

\[
\boxed{
\begin{array}{ll}
\text{If }k\ge r: & n=0,\\[4pt]
\text{If }k<r\text{ and }p>q: &
n=\displaystyle\Bigl\lceil
\frac{\ln\!\bigl(\dfrac{r(100-k)}{k(100-r)}\bigr)}
     {\ln\!\bigl(\dfrac{1-q/100}{1-p/100}\bigr)}
\Bigr\rceil,\\[12pt]
\text{If }k<r\text{ and }p\le q: &
\text{the required percentage cannot be attained.}
\end{array}}
\]

The formula gives the **minimum number of pannings** needed for the gold‑dust to contain at least \(r\%\) pure gold.

Could you help me make sense of this problem? A cubic bottle with side length of 3 centimeters is filled with liquid. When the bottle is placed such that a large diagonal of the cube is perpendicular to the ground, the liquid reaches two-thirds of the length of this diagonal. Determine the fraction of the volume of the bottle that the liquid actually represents.

A concise solution goes like this: Let the cube have side length  

\[
a=3\text{ cm},\qquad\text{so its space diagonal has length }d=a\sqrt3 .
\]

Place the cube so that the space diagonal from the vertex \((0,0,0)\) to the opposite vertex \((a,a,a)\) is vertical.  
The liquid rises a distance  

\[
h=\frac23 d=\frac23 a\sqrt3
\]

measured **along** that diagonal from the bottom vertex.

---

### 1.  Equation of the cutting plane  

A plane perpendicular to the diagonal has normal vector \((1,1,1)\); its equation can be written as  

\[
x+y+z=c .
\]

The distance from the origin to this plane is  

\[
\frac{|c|}{\sqrt{1^2+1^2+1^2}}=\frac{c}{\sqrt3}=h .
\]

Hence  

\[
c = h\sqrt3 = \frac23 a\sqrt3\;\sqrt3 = \frac23 a\cdot 3 = 2a .
\]

So the liquid occupies the region  

\[
\{(x,y,z)\in[0,a]^3\mid x+y+z\le 2a\}.
\]

---

### 2.  Geometry of the cut  

The plane \(x+y+z=2a\) meets the three edges that meet at the opposite corner \((a,a,a)\) at  

\[
(a,a,0),\;(a,0,a),\;(0,a,a).
\]

Thus the part of the cube **above** the plane is a right tetrahedron with orthogonal edges of length \(a\).  
Its volume is  

\[
V_{\text{tetra}}=\frac{1}{6}a^{3}.
\]

The whole cube has volume  

\[
V_{\text{cube}}=a^{3}.
\]

Therefore the volume occupied by the liquid (the part **below** the plane) is  

\[
V_{\text{liq}} = V_{\text{cube}}-V_{\text{tetra}}
               = a^{3}-\frac{1}{6}a^{3}
               = \frac{5}{6}a^{3}.
\]

---

### 3.  Fraction of the bottle filled  

\[
\frac{V_{\text{liq}}}{V_{\text{cube}}}= \frac{5/6\,a^{3}}{a^{3}} = \boxed{\frac56}.
\]

(For the given side length \(a=3\) cm, this corresponds to \(V_{\text{liq}} = \frac56\cdot27 = 22.5\text{ cm}^3\).)

It seems simple, but I'm unsure about the details: Given the Fourier transform of $x(t)$ is $X(\omega)$, find the Fourier transform of $x(-2t+4)$.

Sure, let's start with the idea: The signal  

\[
y(t)=x(-2t+4)
\]

is a time‑scaled and shifted version of \(x(t)\).  
Write the argument as  

\[
-2t+4=-2\bigl(t-2\bigr)
\]

so that  

\[
y(t)=x\!\bigl(-2(t-2)\bigr)=z(t-2),\qquad 
z(t)=x(-2t).
\]

---

### 1.  Scaling  

For a scaling \(z(t)=x(at)\) the Fourier transform is  

\[
Z(\omega)=\frac{1}{|a|}\,X\!\left(\frac{\omega}{a}\right).
\]

With \(a=-2\),

\[
Z(\omega)=\frac{1}{2}\,X\!\left(\frac{\omega}{-2}\right)=\frac{1}{2}\,X\!\left(-\frac{\omega}{2}\right).
\]

---

### 2.  Shifting  

A shift \(y(t)=z(t-t_0)\) multiplies the spectrum by \(e^{-j\omega t_0}\):

\[
Y(\omega)=e^{-j\omega t_0}\,Z(\omega),\qquad t_0=2.
\]

Thus  

\[
Y(\omega)=e^{-j2\omega}\,\frac{1}{2}\,X\!\left(-\frac{\omega}{2}\right).
\]

---

### Result  

\[
\boxed{\,\displaystyle \mathcal{F}\{x(-2t+4)\}=Y(\omega)=\frac{1}{2}\,e^{-j2\omega}\;X\!\Bigl(-\frac{\omega}{2}\Bigr)\,}

\]

Then  

\[
(y+1)^{3}-3(y+1)^{2}-3(y+1)+1=0

\[

Write  

\[
y=2\sqrt{-\frac{p}{3}}\;\cos\theta
   =2\sqrt{2}\;\cos\theta .
\]

Insert this in \(y^{3}+py+q=0\):

(2\sqrt{2}\cos\theta)^{3}-6(2\sqrt{2}\cos\theta)-4=0
\]

Hence  

\[

Starting from basics, how should I solve this? Find all natural numbers \( n \) such that \( n \mid 2^n - 1 \).

Alright, here's a step-by-step explanation: \[
\text{Find all }n\in \mathbb N\text{ such that }n\mid 2^{\,n}-1 .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  Preliminary observations  

*If \(n\) is even and \(n>1\):*  

\(2^{\,n}-1\) is odd, while an even integer \(n>1\) cannot divide an odd number.  
Hence **\(n\) must be odd** (or \(n=1\)).

From now on assume \(n>1\) is odd.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Using the order of \(2\) modulo \(n\)

Because \(\gcd(2,n)=1\), the multiplicative order of \(2\) modulo \(n\) is defined:

\[
\operatorname{ord}_n(2)=d\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad
2^{d}\equiv 1\pmod n,\; d\text{ minimal}.
\]

The hypothesis \(2^{\,n}\equiv 1\pmod n\) tells us that  

\[
d\mid n. \tag{1}
\]

On the other hand, for any integer \(a\) coprime to \(n\) we have  

\[
a^{\lambda(n)}\equiv 1\pmod n,
\]

where \(\lambda(n)\) is the Carmichael function (the exponent of the group
\((\mathbb Z/n\mathbb Z)^{\times}\)).  
Consequently  

\[
d\mid\lambda(n). \tag{2}
\]

From (1) and (2) we obtain  

\[
\lambda(n)\mid n. \tag{3}
\]

Thus a necessary condition for \(n\) to satisfy the problem is that its
Carmichael function divides \(n\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  What does \(\lambda(n)\mid n\) imply?

Write the prime‑power factorisation of an odd integer \(n\):

\[
n=\prod_{i=1}^{k}p_i^{\,e_i},\qquad p_i\ \text{odd primes},\ e_i\ge 1 .
\]

For an odd prime power we have  

\[
\lambda(p_i^{\,e_i})=\varphi(p_i^{\,e_i})=p_i^{\,e_i-1}(p_i-1).
\]

Since \(\lambda(n)=\operatorname{lcm}\bigl(\lambda(p_i^{\,e_i})\bigr)\), condition
(3) forces each \(\lambda(p_i^{\,e_i})\) to divide \(n\).  Hence for every
\(i\)

\[
p_i^{\,e_i-1}(p_i-1)\mid n
      =p_i^{\,e_i}\!\!\!\prod_{j\neq i}p_j^{\,e_j}.
\]

Cancelling the factor \(p_i^{\,e_i-1}\) (which certainly divides the right‑hand
side) we obtain the simpler requirement

\[
p_i-1\mid \prod_{j\neq i}p_j^{\,e_j}= \frac{n}{p_i^{\,e_i}} .\tag{4}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4.  Consequences of (4)

*If \(n\) were a power of a single odd prime* \(p^e\) (\(k=1\)), then (4)
would read \(p-1\mid 1\), i.e. \(p=2\), impossible because we are dealing with
odd numbers.  Hence **\(n\) cannot be a prime power**.

Thus \(k\ge 2\); \(n\) contains at least two distinct odd primes.
Pick the smallest prime divisor \(p\) of \(n\).  
From (4) we have \(p-1\mid n/p^{\,e}\).  The right‑hand side is a product of
odd numbers, therefore it is odd.  But \(p-1\) is **even** (since \(p\) is odd).
An even integer cannot divide an odd integer, a contradiction.

Hence **no odd integer \(n>1\) can satisfy (4)**.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 5.  Conclusion

The only natural number that avoids the contradictions above is  

\[
\boxed{n=1}.
\]

Indeed,
\[
2^{1}-1=1\quad\text{and}\quad 1\mid 1 .
\]

Therefore the complete set of natural numbers \(n\) such that \(n\mid 2^{\,n}-1\)
is \(\{1\}\).

Could we reason through this together: Consider all rational numbers between $0$ and $1$ expressed as fractions in lowest terms. For each such fraction, compute the product of the numerator and the denominator. How many of these products are equal to $2432902008176640000$?

Step by step, this works: The product we are looking at is  

\[
N = 2432902008176640000 = 20!
\]

---

### 1.  Prime factorisation of \(20!\)

\[
\begin{aligned}
20! &= 2^{18}\; 3^{8}\; 5^{4}\; 7^{2}\; 11^{1}\; 13^{1}\; 17^{1}\; 19^{1}.
\end{aligned}
\]

Thus the distinct primes that appear are  

\[
\{2,3,5,7,11,13,17,19\},
\]

i.e. **8 distinct primes**.

---

### 2.  Condition \(\gcd(a,b)=1\)

For a reduced fraction \(\frac{a}{b}\) we must have \(\gcd(a,b)=1\).
If a prime \(p\) divides both \(a\) and \(b\), the fraction would not be in lowest terms.
Hence **each prime factor of \(N\) must be assigned entirely to either \(a\) or \(b\)**—it cannot be split between them.

Consequently, for each of the 8 distinct primes we have two choices:

* give the whole power \(p^{e_p}\) to \(a\), or
* give it to \(b\).

So there are \(2^{8}=256\) ordered pairs \((a,b)\) with \(\gcd(a,b)=1\) and \(ab=N\).

---

### 3.  Ordering condition \(a<b\)

The pair \((a,b)\) and the swapped pair \((b,a)\) give the same reduced fraction, just inverted.
Since \(a\neq b\) (otherwise they would share all primes and could not be coprime unless \(N=1\)), each unordered pair corresponds to exactly two ordered pairs.

Therefore the number of **unordered** coprime factorisations of \(N\) is  

\[
\frac{256}{2}=2^{8-1}=2^{7}=128.
\]

For each unordered pair, exactly one orientation satisfies \(a<b\). Hence the number of reduced fractions \(\frac{a}{b}\) with \(0<a<b\) and \(ab=N\) is also **128**.

---

\[
\boxed{128}
\]
It seems simple, but I'm unsure about the details: Calculate the exact value of the integral $\int^{\pi}_{0}{x^{2}\sin^{2}x}\,dx$.

We can break it down as follows: \[
I=\int_{0}^{\pi}x^{2}\sin ^2x\,dx
\]

Use the double‑angle identity  

\[
\sin ^2x=\frac{1-\cos 2x}{2},
\]

so  

\[
I=\frac12\int_{0}^{\pi}x^{2}\,dx-\frac12\int_{0}^{\pi}x^{2}\cos 2x\,dx
      =\frac{\pi^{3}}{6}-\frac12 J,
\]

where  

\[
J=\int_{0}^{\pi}x^{2}\cos 2x\,dx .
\]

---

### Computing \(J\)

Integrate by parts twice.

1. First integration by parts  

   \[
   u=x^{2},\qquad dv=\cos 2x\,dx\;\Longrightarrow\;
   du=2x\,dx,\; v=\tfrac12\sin 2x.
   \]

   \[
   J=\Bigl[\tfrac12 x^{2}\sin 2x\Bigr]_{0}^{\pi}
      -\int_{0}^{\pi}x\sin 2x\,dx .
   \]

   The boundary term vanishes because \(\sin 2\pi=\sin 0=0\).  
   Hence  

   \[
   J=-\int_{0}^{\pi}x\sin 2x\,dx .
   \]

2. Second integration by parts  

   \[
   u=x,\qquad dv=\sin 2x\,dx\;\Longrightarrow\;
   du=dx,\; v=-\tfrac12\cos 2x.
   \]

   \[
   \int_{0}^{\pi}x\sin 2x\,dx
   =\Bigl[-\tfrac12 x\cos 2x\Bigr]_{0}^{\pi}
     +\tfrac12\int_{0}^{\pi}\cos 2x\,dx .
   \]

   The integral of \(\cos 2x\) over \([0,\pi]\) is zero, and  

   \[
   \Bigl[-\tfrac12 x\cos 2x\Bigr]_{0}^{\pi}
   =-\tfrac12\pi\cos 2\pi =-\frac{\pi}{2}.
   \]

   Therefore  

   \[
   \int_{0}^{\pi}x\sin 2x\,dx = -\frac{\pi}{2},
   \qquad\text{so}\qquad
   J = -\bigl(-\frac{\pi}{2}\bigr)=\frac{\pi}{2}.
   \]

---

### Assemble the result

\[
I=\frac{\pi^{3}}{6}-\frac12\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right)
   =\frac{\pi^{3}}{6}-\frac{\pi}{4}
   =\frac{2\pi^{3}-3\pi}{12}
   =\boxed{\displaystyle \frac{\pi\,(2\pi^{2}-3)}{12}}.
\]

It seems simple, but I'm unsure about the details: Two players $A$ and $B$ alternately take chips from two piles with $a$ and $b$ chips respectively, where initially $a > b$. A move consists of taking from one pile a multiple of the number of chips in the other pile. The winner is the one who takes the last chip from one of the piles. For what value of $\alpha$ can $A$ force a win if initially $a > \alpha b$?

Here's the core idea and its execution: The game is the well‑known **Euclid game**.  
Write the position as an ordered pair \((a,b)\) with \(a>b>0\).  
A move consists of replacing \((a,b)\) by  

\[
(a-kb,\;b)\qquad\text{or}\qquad (a,\;b-ka),
\]

where \(k\ge 1\) is an integer and the new numbers are non‑negative.  
The player who makes one of the numbers equal to \(0\) wins.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  Characterisation of the losing ( \(P\) ) positions  

Let a position be called **cold** (or a \(P\)–position) if the player whose
turn it is to move loses with perfect play.  
If \(a\ge 2b\) the player can remove \(kb\) chips with \(k\ge 2\) and
immediately win, so a cold position must satisfy  

\[
b<a<2b\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad 1<\frac{a}{b}<2 .
\]

Assume \(1<\frac{a}{b}<2\).  
Write \(a=b+r\) with \(0<r<b\). After the only possible move (subtract
\(b\) from the larger pile) the position becomes \((b,r)\).
Hence \((a,b)\) is cold exactly when \((b,r)\) is cold.

Consequently a cold position is obtained by repeatedly applying the
Euclidean algorithm and **always obtaining a quotient equal to 1**.
Thus the continued‑fraction expansion of the ratio \(a/b\) consists only
of 1’s:

\[
\frac{a}{b}= [1;1,1,\dots ,1] = \frac{F_{n+1}}{F_{n}},
\]

where \(F_{k}\) are the Fibonacci numbers.  
All such ratios are approximations of the golden ratio  

\[
\varphi=\frac{1+\sqrt5}{2}=1.618033\ldots .
\]

In fact the set of cold positions is the Beatty pair

\[
\bigl(\,\lfloor k\varphi^{2}\rfloor,\;\lfloor k\varphi\rfloor \bigr),
\qquad k=1,2,3,\dots ,
\]

where the larger component is \(\lfloor k\varphi^{2}\rfloor\) and the
smaller is \(\lfloor k\varphi\rfloor\).  
For every integer pair \((a,b)\) with \(a>b\),

\[
(a,b)\text{ is a }P\text{-position}\iff 
\frac{a}{b}<\varphi .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Winning condition for the first player  

If \(\displaystyle\frac{a}{b}>\varphi\) then the continued fraction of
\(a/b\) contains a quotient \(\ge 2\) at some step of the Euclidean
algorithm. The first player can at that step subtract a suitable multiple
of the smaller pile (at least two copies) and move to a position whose
ratio is \(<\varphi\); that new position is a cold one, so the opponent
has a losing position. Hence the first player can force a win.

Conversely, if \(\displaystyle\frac{a}{b}<\varphi\) the position is already
cold, and any legal move produces a ratio \(> \varphi\), i.e. a winning
position for the opponent. Thus the first player cannot force a win.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  The required constant  

Therefore the first player \(A\) has a forced win **iff**

\[
a>\varphi\,b\qquad\text{where}\qquad 
\boxed{\;\varphi=\frac{1+\sqrt5}{2}\;}
\]

(the golden ratio, approximately \(1.618\)).  

So the required value of \(\alpha\) is \(\displaystyle\alpha=\frac{1+\sqrt5}{2}\).
Could you help me make sense of this problem? Solve the following inequalities. $25^x-2^{2\log _4 6-1}<10\cdot 5^{x-1}$.

Let's outline the key steps: \[
25^{x}-2^{\,2\log _4 6-1}<10\cdot5^{\,x-1}
\]

---

### 1.  Write everything with base \(5\)

\[
25^{x}=(5^{2})^{x}=5^{2x},\qquad 
5^{x-1}=5^{x}\cdot5^{-1}= \frac{5^{x}}5 .
\]

Hence  

\[
5^{2x}-2^{\,2\log _4 6-1}<10\cdot\frac{5^{x}}5
\Longrightarrow 
5^{2x}-2^{\,2\log _4 6-1}<2\cdot5^{x}.
\]

---

### 2.  Introduce a new variable  

Let  

\[
t=5^{x}>0 .
\]

Then \(5^{2x}=t^{2}\) and the inequality becomes  

\[
t^{2}-2t-2^{\,2\log _4 6-1}<0 .
\]

---

### 3.  Evaluate the constant  

\[
2^{\,2\log _4 6-1}=2^{-1}\cdot2^{\,2\log _4 6}
               =\frac12\Bigl(2^{\log _4 6}\Bigr)^{2}.
\]

Since  

\[
2^{\log _4 6}=2^{\frac12\log _2 6}=6^{1/2}=\sqrt6,
\]

we have  

\[
2^{\,2\log _4 6-1}= \frac12\bigl(\sqrt6\bigr)^{2}= \frac12\cdot6=3.
\]

Thus  

\[
t^{2}-2t-3<0.
\]

---

### 4.  Solve the quadratic inequality  

\[
t^{2}-2t-3=(t-3)(t+1)<0.
\]

The product of two factors is negative when the factors have opposite signs.  
Because \(t>0\), the factor \(t+1\) is always positive, so we need  

\[
t-3<0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad 0<t<3.
\]

---

### 5.  Return to \(x\)

\[
0<5^{x}<3\quad\Longrightarrow\quad x<\log_{5}3.
\]

There is no lower bound ( \(5^{x}>0\) for every real \(x\) ), so the solution set is  

\[
\boxed{\,x<\log_{5}3\,}.
\]

In interval notation: \((-\infty,\;\log_{5}3)\).

Could you walk me through it step by step? In a square pyramid with base side length \( a = 12 \) and slant height \( S = 2\sqrt{34} \), a cube is placed such that its top face touches each of the pyramid's triangular sides. Calculate the volume of the cube.

Let's outline the key steps: **Step 1 – Find the height of the pyramid**

For a square pyramid the slant height \(S\) (the distance from the midpoint of a base side to the apex) satisfies  

\[
S^{2}=H^{2}+\left(\frac{a}{2}\right)^{2},
\]

where \(H\) is the vertical height of the pyramid and \(a\) is the side of the base.

\[
\begin{aligned}
S &=2\sqrt{34},\qquad a=12\;\Longrightarrow\; \frac{a}{2}=6,\\[2mm]
(2\sqrt{34})^{2}&=H^{2}+6^{2}\\
136&=H^{2}+36\\
H^{2}&=100\;\Longrightarrow\; H=10 .
\end{aligned}
\]

So the pyramid is \(10\) units tall.

--------------------------------------------------------------------

**Step 2 – Set up a coordinate system**

Place the centre of the square base at the origin, the base in the plane \(z=0\) and the apex at \((0,0,10)\).

The four triangular faces are then

\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{East face:}&\; x = 6-\frac{3}{5}z,\\
\text{West face:}&\; x = -6+\frac{3}{5}z,\\
\text{North face:}&\; y = 6-\frac{3}{5}z,\\
\text{South face:}&\; y = -6+\frac{3}{5}z .
\end{aligned}
\]

(These follow because at the base (\(z=0\)) the faces meet the lines \(x=\pm6\) or \(y=\pm6\), and at the apex (\(z=10\)) they meet the centre \((0,0)\).)

--------------------------------------------------------------------

**Step 3 – Geometry of the inscribed cube**

The cube sits on the base of the pyramid, its faces are parallel to the base, and its top face is *rotated* \(45^{\circ}\) so that each vertex of the top face touches a different triangular side.

If the side length of the cube is \(x\), the top face is at height \(z=x\).  
The four vertices of the top face are therefore

\[
\left(\frac{x}{2},0,x\right),\;
\left(-\frac{x}{2},0,x\right),\;
\left(0,\frac{x}{2},x\right),\;
\left(0,-\frac{x}{2},x\right).
\]

Each of these points must satisfy the equation of the corresponding face.  
Take the vertex \(\bigl(\frac{x}{2},0,x\bigr)\) on the east face:

\[
\frac{x}{2}=6-\frac{3}{5}x .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------

**Step 4 – Solve for the cube’s side length**

\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{x}{2}&=6-\frac{3}{5}x\\[2mm]
\frac{5x}{10}&=6-\frac{6x}{10}\\[2mm]
11x&=60\\[2mm]
x&=\frac{60}{11}.
\end{aligned}
\]

Thus the cube’s side length is \(\displaystyle x=\frac{60}{11}\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------

**Step 5 – Volume of the cube**

\[
V = x^{3}= \left(\frac{60}{11}\right)^{3}
      = \frac{60^{3}}{11^{3}}
      = \frac{216\,000}{1331}\;\text{cubic units}.
\]

Numerically,
\[
V \approx 162.3\ \text{units}^{3}.
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------

\[
\boxed{V=\dfrac{216\,000}{1331}\ \text{(approximately }162.3\text{)}} 
\]
Could you help me make sense of this problem? Find all nonnegative integers \( m \) and \( n \) such that \( 1! \cdot 3! \cdot 5! \cdots (2n-1)! = m! \).

Sure, let's start with the idea: \[
P(n)=1!\cdot 3!\cdot 5!\cdots (2n-1)!\qquad (n\ge 0)
\]

We have to determine all pairs \((m,n)\in \mathbb Z_{\ge 0}^{2}\) for which  

\[
P(n)=m!.
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  Small values  

\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c}
n & P(n) & \text{factorial?} \\ \hline
0 & 1 & 0!=1,\;1!=1\\
1 & 1! =1 & 1!\\
2 & 1!\,3! =6 & 3!\\
3 & 1!\,3!\,5! =720 & 6!\\
4 & 1!\,3!\,5!\,7! =3628800 & 10!
\end{array}
\]

Thus  

\[
(m,n)=(0,0),\;(1,0),\;(1,1),\;(3,2),\;(6,3),\;(10,4)
\]

satisfy the required equality.  
We shall now show that **no further solutions exist**.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  A useful notation  

Denote  

\[
T_n=\frac{n(n+1)}2\qquad (n\ge 0)
\]

(the \(n\)-th triangular number).  
From the table we see that for \(n=0,1,2,3,4\)

\[
P(n)=T_n!\; .
\tag{1}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  How the product grows  

For \(n\ge 1\)

\[
P(n+1)=P(n)\,(2n+1)! .
\tag{2}
\]

On the other hand  

\[
T_{n+1}=T_n+(n+1),\qquad 
\frac{T_{n+1}!}{T_n!}= \prod_{i=1}^{\,n+1}\bigl(T_n+i\bigr).
\tag{3}
\]

Consequently, using (2) and (3),

\[
\frac{P(n+1)}{T_{n+1}!}
   =\frac{(2n+1)!}{\displaystyle\prod_{i=1}^{\,n+1}(T_n+i)} .
\tag{4}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4.  The ratio \((2n+1)! / \prod_{i=1}^{n+1}(T_n+i)\)

For \(n\ge 4\) we have  

\[
2n+1\ge n+5\qquad\text{and}\qquad T_n=\frac{n(n+1)}2\ge 10 .
\]

Hence each factor of the product in the denominator is at most
\(T_n+n+1\le 2n+1\) and at least \(T_n+1\ge n+5\).  
A direct comparison gives

\[
\boxed{\;
\prod_{i=1}^{\,n+1}(T_n+i)\;<\;(2n+1)!\;<\;(T_n+n+2)\,
\prod_{i=1}^{\,n+1}(T_n+i)
\qquad (n\ge 4)
\;}
\tag{5}
\]

(The left‑hand inequality is true for \(n=4\) because  
\(9!=362\,880\) and \(\prod_{i=1}^{5}(10+i)=11\cdot12\cdot13\cdot14\cdot15=360\,360\);  
the right‑hand inequality follows from the same calculation for
\(n+1\).)

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 5.  Consequences for \(P(n)\)

From (4) and (5) we obtain, for every \(n\ge 4\),

\[
T_{n+1}! \;<\; P(n+1) \;<\; (T_{n+1}+1)! .
\tag{6}
\]

Thus \(P(n+1)\) lies strictly between two consecutive factorials,
hence it cannot itself be a factorial.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 6.  Completion of the proof  

We have shown

* for \(n=0,1,2,3,4\) the equality \(P(n)=T_n!\) holds (see the table);
* for every \(n\ge 5\) the inequality (6) holds, so \(P(n)\) is **not**
  a factorial.

Therefore the only pairs \((m,n)\) with \(P(n)=m!\) are those obtained
from the table.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 7.  Final answer  

\[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
&(m,n)=(0,0),\;(1,0),\;(1,1),\;(3,2),\;(6,3),\;(10,4).
\end{aligned}}
\]

(If one wishes to exclude the trivial case \(n=0\), the solutions are
\((m,n)=(1,1),\;(3,2),\;(6,3),\;(10,4)\).)

Hi, I have a question: Given a cube $ABCDA_1B_1C_1D_1$ $(AA_1\| BB_1\| CC_1\| DD_1)$. Points $M$ and $N$ are taken on the extensions of the edges $AB$ and $BB_1$ respectively, the points being such that $|AM|=|B_1N|=\frac{1}{2}|AB|$, $(|BM|=|BN|=\frac{3}{2}|AB|)$. Where, on the edge $CC_1$, must the point $P$ lie for a pentagon to result in the section of the cube by a plane drawn through the points $M$, $N$ and $P$?

Sure, let's start with the idea: Let the side of the cube be \(a\;(=|AB|)\) and put a Cartesian system with  

\[
A(0,0,0),\;B(a,0,0),\;C(a,a,0),\;D(0,a,0),\qquad 
A_{1}(0,0,a),\;B_{1}(a,0,a),\;C_{1}(a,a,a),\;D_{1}(0,a,a).
\]

---

### The points \(M\) and \(N\)

* \(M\) lies on the extension of \(AB\) beyond \(A\) and \(|AM|=\frac12 a\); hence  

\[
M\Bigl(-\frac a2,0,0\Bigr).
\]

* \(N\) lies on the extension of \(BB_{1}\) beyond \(B_{1}\) and \(|B_{1}N|=\frac12 a\); therefore  

\[
N\Bigl(a,0,\frac32 a\Bigr).
\]

---

### The point \(P\) on \(CC_{1}\)

Write \(P\) as  

\[
P\bigl(a,a,t\bigr),\qquad 0\le t\le a .
\]

---

### Equation of the plane \((MNP)\)

Two direction vectors are  

\[
\vec{v}_{1}=N-M=\Bigl(\frac{3a}{2},0,\frac{3a}{2}\Bigr),\qquad 
\vec{v}_{2}=P-M=\Bigl(\frac{3a}{2},a,t\Bigr).
\]

A normal vector is  

\[
\vec n=\vec v_{1}\times\vec v_{2}
      =\Bigl(-\frac{3a^{2}}{2},\;-\frac{3a^{2}}{2}\frac{t}{a}+ \frac{9a^{2}}{4},\;
        \frac{3a^{2}}{2}\Bigr)
      =\Bigl(-\frac32,\;-\frac32\frac{t}{a}+ \frac94,\;\frac32\Bigr)a^{2}.
\]

Dividing by \(\frac32 a^{2}\) we obtain the plane in the convenient form  

\[
-2x-1+(-2\frac{t}{a}+3)\,y+2z=0\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad
f(x,y,z)= -2x-1+(-2\frac{t}{a}+3)y+2z .
\]

---

### Intersections with the cube

Evaluate \(f\) at the eight vertices:

\[
\begin{array}{c|c}
\text{Vertex} & f \\ \hline
A(0,0,0) & -1\\
B(a,0,0) & -3\\
C(a,a,0) & -2t\\
D(0,a,0) & 2-2t\\
A_{1}(0,0,a) & 1\\
B_{1}(a,0,a) & -1\\
C_{1}(a,a,a) & 2-2t\\
D_{1}(0,a,a) & 4-2t
\end{array}
\]

For \(0<t<a\) the signs are  

\[
\begin{aligned}
&f<0 \text{ at }A,B,C,B_{1},\\
&f>0 \text{ at }A_{1},D,D_{1},C_{1},
\end{aligned}
\]

so the plane cuts the six edges  

\[
CD,\;DA,\;AA_{1},\;A_{1}B_{1},\;B_{1}C_{1},\;CC_{1},
\]

giving **six** intersection points – a hexagon.

To obtain a pentagon one of these intersection points must coincide with a vertex of the cube, i.e. the plane must pass through a vertex.  
From the table this happens only when  

* \(t=0\) (\(P=C\)), because then \(f(C)=0\);
* \(t=a\) (\(P=C_{1}\)), because then \(f(D)=f(C_{1})=0\).

In each of these two cases two of the above edges meet at the same vertex, so the section has **five** distinct vertices – a pentagon.

---

## Answer

The section is a pentagon only when the point \(P\) coincides with an end of the edge \(CC_{1}\); i.e.

\[
\boxed{P=C\quad\text{or}\quad P=C_{1}} .
\]

Equivalently, the required position of \(P\) on \(CC_{1}\) is at a distance \(0\) from \(C\) (or a distance \(a\) from \(C\)), i.e. \(CP:PC_{1}=0:1\) or \(1:0\). Any interior point of \(CC_{1}\) would give a hexagonal section.
How would you approach this? $\left(\sin 2x+\sqrt 3\cos 2x\right)^2-5=\cos \left(\frac{\pi }{6}-2x\right)$.

First the conclusion, then the reasoning: \[
\bigl(\sin 2x+\sqrt3\cos 2x\bigr)^2-5=\cos\!\Bigl(\frac{\pi}{6}-2x\Bigr)
\qquad (x\in\mathbb R)
\]

---

### 1.  Simplify the left–hand side  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\bigl(\sin 2x+\sqrt3\cos 2x\bigr)^2
&=\sin ^2 2x+3\cos ^2 2x+2\sqrt3\sin 2x\cos 2x\\
&=1+2\cos ^2 2x+2\sqrt3\sin 2x\cos 2x\\[2mm]
&=1+(1+\cos 4x)+\sqrt3\sin 4x\\
&=2+\cos 4x+\sqrt3\sin 4x .
\end{aligned}
\]

Hence  

\[
\bigl(\sin 2x+\sqrt3\cos 2x\bigr)^2-5
= -3+\cos 4x+\sqrt3\sin 4x .
\]

Write the combination of \(\cos 4x\) and \(\sin 4x\) as a single cosine:

\[
\cos 4x+\sqrt3\sin 4x
=2\cos\!\bigl(4x-\tfrac{\pi}{3}\bigr),
\]

because \(\sqrt{1^2+(\sqrt3)^2}=2\) and the phase shift is \(\phi=\pi/3\).

Thus  

\[
\text{LHS}= -3+2\cos\!\bigl(4x-\tfrac{\pi}{3}\bigr).
\]

---

### 2.  Simplify the right–hand side  

\[
\cos\!\Bigl(\frac{\pi}{6}-2x\Bigr)
= \frac{\sqrt3}{2}\cos 2x+\frac12\sin 2x
= \cos\!\bigl(2x-\tfrac{\pi}{6}\bigr).
\]

---

### 3.  Reduce to a single variable  

Set  

\[
\theta = 2x-\frac{\pi}{6}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
4x-\frac{\pi}{3}=2\theta .
\]

The equation becomes  

\[
2\cos(2\theta)-\cos\theta-3=0 .
\]

Use \(\cos 2\theta = 2\cos^2\theta-1\):

\[
2\bigl(2\cos^2\theta-1\bigr)-\cos\theta-3=0
\Longrightarrow 4\cos^2\theta-\cos\theta-5=0 .
\]

Let \(y=\cos\theta\). Then  

\[
4y^{2}-y-5=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
y=\frac{1\pm\sqrt{1+80}}{8}
   =\frac{1\pm9}{8}.
\]

Hence  

\[
y_1=\frac{10}{8}= \frac54\;(>1\text{, impossible}),\qquad
y_2=-1 .
\]

So the only admissible value is  

\[
\cos\theta = -1\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\theta = \pi+2k\pi,\qquad k\in\mathbb Z .
\]

Recall \(\theta = 2x-\dfrac{\pi}{6}\); therefore  

\[
2x-\frac{\pi}{6}= \pi+2k\pi
\Longrightarrow 2x = \frac{7\pi}{6}+2k\pi

\]

For \(x=\dfrac{7\pi}{12}\) (the case \(k=0\)):

\[

\bigl(\cdot\bigr)^2-5 =4-5=-1,\\
\cos\!\Bigl(\frac{\pi}{6}-2x\Bigr)&=\cos\!\Bigl(\frac{\pi}{6}-\frac{7\pi}{6}\Bigr)
 =\cos(-\pi)= -1 .
\end{aligned}
\]

Both sides coincide; the same holds for every \(x\) of the form \( \frac{7\pi}{12}+k\pi\).

\boxed{\displaystyle x = \frac{7\pi}{12}+k\pi,\qquad k\in\mathbb Z}

Could we reason through this together: Two bugs are placed at opposite vertices of a regular octahedron. Each day, each bug randomly selects with equal probability one of the adjacent vertices and walks along the edge connecting the two vertices. If $\mathbb{E}$ is the expected number of days it will take for the two bugs to meet each other for the first time, compute $\lfloor 10 \mathbb{E} \rfloor$.

Let's outline the key steps: Let the vertices of the regular octahedron be the six points  

\[
(\pm1,0,0),\;(0,\pm1,0),\;(0,0,\pm1)
\]

and join two vertices by an edge when their dot product is \(0\).  
Each vertex has degree \(4\); the graph is the complete graph \(K_6\) with the three opposite edges removed.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  Distances between the bugs  

Only three distances are possible:

* \(0\) – the bugs are on the same vertex (they have met);
* \(1\) – the bugs are on adjacent vertices;
* \(2\) – the bugs are on opposite vertices.

The bugs start at distance \(2\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Transition probabilities  

Denote by \(p_{ij}\) the probability that the distance changes from \(i\) to \(j\) after one day.

---

#### From distance \(2\) (opposite vertices)

Both bugs must move to one of the four vertices that are adjacent to **both** of the opposite vertices.

* They land on the same vertex: probability \(\displaystyle 4\left(\frac14\right)^2=\frac14\).
* They land on two different vertices that are adjacent to each other: probability \(\displaystyle\frac12\).
* They land on two different vertices that are opposite to each other: probability \(\displaystyle\frac14\).

Hence  

\[
p_{20}= \frac14,\qquad p_{21}= \frac12,\qquad p_{22}= \frac14 .
\]

---

#### From distance \(1\) (adjacent vertices)

Let the bugs be at vertices \(u\) and \(v\) with \(uv\) an edge.  
Each has four neighbours; the two common neighbours are the only vertices adjacent to **both** \(u\) and \(v\).

* Both move to the same common neighbour: probability  
  \(2\left(\frac14\right)^2 = \frac18\) → distance \(0\).
* They move to the two different common neighbours (which are opposite): probability  
  \(2\left(\frac14\right)^2 = \frac18\) → distance \(2\).
* All other possibilities (the remaining \(12\) ordered pairs) give vertices that are adjacent → distance \(1\).

Thus  

\[
p_{10}= \frac18,\qquad p_{11}= \frac34,\qquad p_{12}= \frac18 .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Expected hitting times  

Let \(E_0=0\) (already met), \(E_1\) be the expected remaining days when the bugs are at distance \(1\), and \(E_2\) when they are at distance \(2\).

From the transition probabilities:

\[
\begin{aligned}
E_1 &= 1 + p_{10}E_0 + p_{11}E_1 + p_{12}E_2
      = 1 + \frac34E_1 + \frac18E_2,\\[2mm]
E_2 &= 1 + p_{20}E_0 + p_{21}E_1 + p_{22}E_2
      = 1 + \frac12E_1 + \frac14E_2 .
\end{aligned}
\]

Solving,

\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac14E_1 &= 1 + \frac18E_2 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
E_1 = 4 + \frac12E_2,\\[2mm]
\frac34E_2 &= 1 + \frac12E_1 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
E_2 = \frac{4}{3} + \frac23E_1 .
\end{aligned}
\]

Substituting the first into the second:

\[
E_2 = \frac{4}{3} + \frac23\!\left(4+\frac12E_2\right)
     = 4 + \frac13E_2 \;\Longrightarrow\; \frac23E_2 = 4
     \;\Longrightarrow\; E_2 = 6 .
\]

Thus the expected number of days for the bugs to meet, starting from opposite vertices, is  

\[
\boxed{E = 6}.
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4.  Required integer

\[
\left\lfloor 10E \right\rfloor = \left\lfloor 10 \times 6 \right\rfloor = 60 .
\]

\[
\boxed{60}
\]
What would be a clean way to solve this? $\sqrt {-3\sin 5x-\cos ^2 x-3}+\sin x=1$.

Alright, here's a step-by-step explanation: \[
\sqrt{-3\sin 5x-\cos ^2x-3}+\sin x =1\qquad (1)
\]

---

### 1.  Put the radical on one side  

\[
\sqrt{-3\sin 5x-\cos ^2x-3}=1-\sin x .
\]

Since a square‑root is non‑negative we must have  

\[
1-\sin x\ge 0\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \sin x\le 1,
\]

which is always true, but we also need the radicand to be non‑negative.

---

### 2.  Express the radicand with \(\sin x\)

\[
\begin{aligned}
-3\sin 5x-\cos ^2x-3
&=-3\sin 5x-(1-\sin ^2x)-3\\
&=\sin ^2x-3\sin 5x-4 .
\end{aligned}
\]

Hence  

\[
\sqrt{\sin ^2x-3\sin 5x-4}=1-\sin x. \tag{2}
\]

---

### 3.  Square (2)

\[
\sin ^2x-3\sin 5x-4=(1-\sin x)^2
      =1-2\sin x+\sin ^2x .
\]

Cancel \(\sin ^2x\) :

\[
-3\sin 5x-4=1-2\sin x\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\sin 5x=\frac{2\sin x-5}{3}. \tag{3}
\]

---

### 4.  Use the identity for \(\sin 5x\)

\[
\sin 5x=16\sin ^5x-20\sin ^3x+5\sin x .
\]

Insert this into (3) and set \(s=\sin x\):

\[
16s^{5}-20s^{3}+5s=\frac{2s-5}{3}.
\]

Multiplying by \(3\) gives a quintic polynomial

\[
48s^{5}-60s^{3}+13s+5=0. \tag{4}
\]

---

### 5.  Show that (4) has **no** real root in \([-1,1]\)

Define  

\[
f(s)=48s^{5}-60s^{3}+13s+5 .
\]

Its derivative  

\[
f'(s)=240s^{4}-180s^{2}+13
\]

vanishes only at  

\[
s^{2}= \frac{180\pm\sqrt{180^{2}-4\cdot240\cdot13}}{2\cdot240}
      \approx 0.0808\quad\text{or}\quad 0.669 .
\]

Thus the critical points are \(s\approx\pm0.284,\;\pm0.818\).
Evaluating \(f\) at these points:

\[
\begin{aligned}
f(0.284)&\approx 7.41,\\
f(0.818)&\approx 0.33,\\
f(-0.284)&\approx 7.41,\\
f(-0.818)&\approx 9.67 .
\end{aligned}
\]

The global minimum of \(f\) on \([-1,1]\) is about \(0.33>0\); hence  

\[
f(s)>0\qquad\text{for all }s\in[-1,1].
\]

Consequently equation (4) has **no** real solution for \(s=\sin x\).

---

### 6.  Check the possibility that the radicand is zero  

Because a square‑root is defined only when its argument is non‑negative,
from (2) we must have  

\[
\sin ^2x-3\sin 5x-4\ge 0 .
\]

But \(\sin ^2x\le 1\) and \(-3\sin 5x\le 3\); therefore  

\[
\sin ^2x-3\sin 5x-4\le 1+3-4=0 .
\]

Hence the radicand can be non‑negative **only** when it is exactly zero:

\[
\sin ^2x-3\sin 5x-4=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\sin 5x=-1,\;\sin ^2x=1 .
\]

The only possibilities are \(\sin x=1\) or \(\sin x=-1\).

* If \(\sin x=1\) (\(x=\frac{\pi}{2}+2k\pi\)), then \(\sin 5x=1\neq-1\) – the radicand is \(-6\).
* If \(\sin x=-1\) (\(x=\frac{3\pi}{2}+2k\pi\)), then \(\sin 5x=-1\) and the radicand is \(0\), but the original equation becomes \(\;0+(-1)=1\), i.e. \(-1=1\), which is false.

Thus even the borderline case gives no solution.

---

## Conclusion

The original equation has **no real solution**.

\[
\boxed{\text{No real }x\text{ satisfies }\sqrt{-3\sin 5x-\cos ^2x-3}+\sin x =1.}
\]

I'd like to verify my understanding—how do we solve this: Let \( p \) be a prime number, \( q \geq 1 \), \( n \geq 2 \) be integers, and \( K = \mathbb{F}_p \). Let \( A \in M_n(K) \) be a matrix with \( n \) distinct eigenvalues in the algebraic closure of \( K \). Find all matrices \( X \in M_n(K) \) such that \( X^{(p^q)} = A \).

Here's a clear solution: Let  

\[
K=\mathbb F_{p},\qquad X\in M_{n}(K),\qquad A\in M_{n}(K)
\]

and denote by  

\[
X^{(p^{q})}:=\bigl(x_{ij}^{\,p^{q}}\bigr)_{1\le i,j\le n}
\]

the matrix obtained by raising **each entry** of \(X\) to the \(p^{q}\)-th power
(the Frobenius endomorphism of the matrix algebra).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  The Frobenius map on \(\mathbb F_{p}\) is the identity  

For any \(a\in\mathbb F_{p}\) we have  

\[
a^{p}=a\qquad\text{(Fermat’s little theorem)},
\]

hence inductively  

\[
a^{p^{q}}=a\qquad\text{for every }q\ge 1 .
\]

Consequently the map  

\[
\varphi_{q}:K\longrightarrow K,\qquad a\mapsto a^{p^{q}}
\]

is the identity on the whole field \(K\).  
Since \(\varphi_{q}\) is applied entry‑wise, it is also the identity on the
matrix algebra \(M_{n}(K)\):

\[
X^{(p^{q})}=X\qquad\text{for every }X\in M_{n}(K).
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Solving the equation  

The required matrices satisfy  

\[
X^{(p^{q})}=A .
\]

Because the left–hand side equals \(X\) for any \(X\in M_{n}(K)\), the
equation reduces to  

\[
X=A .
\]

Thus **the only matrix in \(M_{n}(K)\) whose entrywise \(p^{q}\)-th power
equals \(A\) is \(A\) itself**.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Remarks  

* The hypothesis that \(A\) has \(n\) distinct eigenvalues (hence is
  diagonalizable over \(\overline K\)) is not needed for the conclusion;
  it only guarantees that \(A\) is “nice’’ but does not affect the
  Frobenius computation.

* If one allowed matrices with entries in a larger field (for instance in
  \(\overline K\)), then each entry of \(A\) would have exactly \(p^{q}\)
  distinct \(p^{q}\)-th roots, giving \(p^{qn}\) solutions.  Over the
  ground field \(\mathbb F_{p}\) the Frobenius map is the identity, so
  only the trivial solution remains.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
\[
\boxed{\;X=A\;}
\]

Alright, here's a step-by-step explanation: **Given data**

\[
AC=BC,\qquad \angle ACB =100^{\circ}
\]

Hence  

\[
\angle CAB=\angle CBA=\frac{180^{\circ}-100^{\circ}}2=40^{\circ}.
\]

The point \(D\) lies on the line \(AC\) beyond \(A\) (the order of the points is \(C-A-D\) ) and  

\[
CD = AB .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 1.  Lengths on the line \(AC\)

Take \(AC=BC=1\) (any convenient unit).  
From the law of cosines in \(\triangle ABC\)

\[
AB^{2}=AC^{2}+BC^{2}-2\cdot AC\cdot BC\cos 100^{\circ}
      =2-2\cos 100^{\circ}.
\]

Because \(CD=AB\) and \(CD=CA+AD\),

\[
AD = CD-CA = AB-AC = AB-1 .
\]

Thus  

\[
AD = \sqrt{2-2\cos 100^{\circ}}-1 .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 2.  The angle \(\angle BAD\)

The ray \(AD\) is the continuation of \(CA\) beyond \(A\); therefore it forms the **exterior** angle at \(A\) of \(\triangle ABC\):

\[
\boxed{\;\angle BAD = 180^{\circ}-\angle CAB = 180^{\circ}-40^{\circ}=140^{\circ}\;}
\]

Apply the law of cosines in \(\triangle ABD\) with the known side lengths
\(AB,\;AD\) and the included angle \(140^{\circ}\):

\[
\begin{aligned}
BD^{2}&=AB^{2}+AD^{2}-2\;AB\;AD\cos 140^{\circ}\\
      &=AB^{2}+AD^{2}+2\;AB\;AD\cos 40^{\circ}
\end{aligned}
\]

( because \(\cos 140^{\circ}= -\cos 40^{\circ}\) ).

A short computation gives  

\[
BD^{2}=3.873\ldots\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad BD\approx1.969 .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 4.  Remaining angles of \(\triangle ABD\)

Use the law of sines:

\[
\frac{\sin\angle ABD}{AD}= \frac{\sin\angle BAD}{BD}
      =\frac{\sin 140^{\circ}}{BD}.
\]

Since \(\sin 140^{\circ}= \sin 40^{\circ}\),

\[
\sin\angle ABD = AD\;\frac{\sin 40^{\circ}}{BD}
               \approx 0.1732 .

\[
\boxed{\;\angle ABD \approx 10^{\circ}\;}

(the acute solution, because the sum of the three angles must be \(180^{\circ}\)).

Finally  

\[

\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 5.  Result

\[
\boxed{\displaystyle
\angle ABD = 10^{\circ},\qquad

It seems simple, but I'm unsure about the details: From all the triangles with the same base and the same vertex angle $\alpha $ choose the triangle with the greatest perimeter.

Alright, here's a step-by-step explanation: Let  

\[
BC=a\qquad\text{(the base is fixed)},\qquad \angle BAC=\alpha\;(0<\alpha<\pi)
\]

and let \(A\) move while the base \(BC\) and the angle \(\alpha\) stay unchanged.
Denote by \(P\) the perimeter of \(\triangle ABC\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  The circum‑circle is fixed  

From the law of sines  

\[
\frac{a}{\sin\alpha}=2R ,
\]

hence the circum‑radius  

\[
R=\frac{a}{2\sin\alpha}
\]

is the same for every admissible triangle.  
Consequently the vertex \(A\) must lie on the circle of radius \(R\) that
passes through the fixed points \(B\) and \(C\).  
All such triangles have the same circum‑circle; the chord \(BC\) subtends
the central angle  

\[
\widehat{BOC}=2\alpha .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Express \(AB+AC\) as a function of the position of \(A\)

Place the centre \(O\) of the circle at the origin and let the chord
\(BC\) be symmetric with respect to the \(x\)-axis:

\[
B\;(R\cos\alpha,\,-R\sin\alpha),\qquad 
C\;(R\cos\alpha,\, R\sin\alpha).
\]

Write \(A\) in polar coordinates \(A(R\cos\varphi,R\sin\varphi)\)
(\(\varphi\neq\pm\alpha\)).  Using  

\[
AB^{2}=R^{2}\bigl[(\cos\varphi-\cos\alpha)^{2}+(\sin\varphi+\sin\alpha)^{2}\bigr]
      =2R^{2}\bigl[1-\cos(\varphi+\alpha)\bigr],
\]

\[
AC^{2}=2R^{2}\bigl[1-\cos(\varphi-\alpha)\bigr],
\]

we obtain  

\[
AB=2R\sin\frac{\varphi+\alpha}{2},\qquad
AC=2R\sin\frac{\varphi-\alpha}{2}.
\]

Hence  

\[
AB+AC=2R\Bigl[\sin\frac{\varphi+\alpha}{2}+\sin\frac{\varphi-\alpha}{2}\Bigr]
     =4R\cos\frac{\alpha}{2}\,\sin\frac{\varphi}{2}.
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Maximising the sum  

For the fixed data \(a,\alpha\) the factors \(4R\cos\frac{\alpha}{2}\) are
constants.  The only variable factor is \(\sin\frac{\varphi}{2}\), whose
maximum value is \(1\).  This occurs when  

\[
\frac{\varphi}{2}= \frac{\pi}{2}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \varphi=\pi .
\]

Thus the maximum of \(AB+AC\) is attained at the point of the circle
opposite the chord \(BC\); i.e. when \(A\) lies on the line \(OM\) (the
perpendicular bisector of \(BC\)) on the side of \(O\) opposite to the
base.  In that position  

\[
AB=AC=2R\cos\frac{\alpha}{2}.
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4.  The triangle of greatest perimeter  

The triangle with the greatest perimeter is therefore the **isosceles**
triangle for which the vertex \(A\) is diametrically opposite the midpoint
of the base.  Its sides are  

\[
BC=a,\qquad AB=AC=2R\cos\frac{\alpha}{2}
          =\frac{a}{2\sin\frac{\alpha}{2}} .
\]

Consequently the maximal perimeter is  

\[
\boxed{P_{\max}=a+2\cdot\frac{a}{2\sin\frac{\alpha}{2}}
        =a\Bigl(1+\csc\frac{\alpha}{2}\Bigr)} .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
**Answer.**  
Among all triangles having a given base \(BC\) and a given vertex angle
\(\alpha\) at the opposite vertex, the perimeter is largest for the
isosceles triangle whose vertex lies on the extension of the perpendicular
bisector of the base, i.e. for the triangle with  

\[
AB=AC=\frac{a}{2\sin(\alpha/2)} .
\]

Its perimeter equals \(a\bigl(1+\csc(\alpha/2)\bigr)\).

Can you outline a strategy for this question? You roll a die, and I roll a die. You win if the number showing on your die is strictly greater than the one on mine. If we play the game five times, what is the probability that you win at least 4 times?

Let's outline the key steps: **Step 1 – Probability of a win in a single game**

When two fair six‑sided dice are rolled, the ordered pairs \((i,j)\) with  
\(i\) = your die, \(j\) = my die are equally likely \((36\) possibilities).

You win when \(i>j\).

\[
\begin{aligned}
\#\{i>j\}&=\sum_{j=1}^{5}(6-j)=5+4+3+2+1=15 .
\end{aligned}
\]

Hence  

\[
p=\Pr(\text{you win a single game})=\frac{15}{36}=\frac{5}{12},
\qquad
q=1-p=\frac{7}{12}.
\]

(If the dice are equal you do **not** win, so a tie counts as a loss for the purpose of “wins”.)

---

**Step 2 – Model the five games**

The five games are independent, so the number of wins \(X\) follows a binomial distribution  

\[
X\sim\operatorname{Binomial}(n=5,\;p=\tfrac{5}{12}).
\]

We need  

\[
\Pr(X\ge 4)=\Pr(X=4)+\Pr(X=5).
\]

---

**Step 3 – Compute the two terms**

\[
\begin{aligned}
\Pr(X=4) &= \binom{5}{4}p^{4}q^{1}
          =5\left(\frac{5}{12}\right)^{4}\left(\frac{7}{12}\right),\\[4pt]
\Pr(X=5) &= \binom{5}{5}p^{5}
          =\left(\frac{5}{12}\right)^{5}.
\end{aligned}
\]

Calculate:

\[
\begin{aligned}
\Pr(X=4) &=5\cdot\frac{5^{4}}{12^{4}}\cdot\frac{7}{12}
          =5\cdot\frac{625}{20736}\cdot\frac{7}{12}
          =\frac{21\,875}{248\,832},\\[4pt]
\Pr(X=5) &=\frac{5^{5}}{12^{5}}
          =\frac{3\,125}{248\,832}.
\end{aligned}
\]

---

**Step 4 – Add them**

\[
\Pr(X\ge 4)=\frac{21\,875+3\,125}{248\,832}
           =\frac{25\,000}{248\,832}
           =\frac{3\,125}{31\,104}\approx0.1005.
\]

---

\[
\boxed{\displaystyle \Pr(\text{at least 4 wins in 5 games})=\frac{3125}{31104}\approx10.0\%}
\]
Could we reason through this together: Calculate the integral $\int \ln(x^2 - x + 1) \, dx$.

Here's a clear solution: \[
\int \ln (x^{2}-x+1)\,dx
\]

Use integration by parts  

\[
u=\ln (x^{2}-x+1),\qquad dv=dx\;\Longrightarrow\;
du=\frac{2x-1}{x^{2}-x+1}\,dx,\qquad v=x .
\]

\[
\begin{aligned}
\int\ln (x^{2}-x+1)\,dx
&=x\ln (x^{2}-x+1)-\int x\frac{2x-1}{x^{2}-x+1}\,dx   \\
&=x\ln Q-\int\frac{2x^{2}-x}{Q}\,dx ,
\qquad Q:=x^{2}-x+1 .
\end{aligned}
\]

Divide the rational function:

\[
\frac{2x^{2}-x}{Q}=2+\frac{x-2}{Q},
\]

so that  

\[
\int\frac{2x^{2}-x}{Q}\,dx=2x+\int\frac{x-2}{Q}\,dx .
\]

Write the remaining numerator as a combination of the derivative of \(Q\) and a constant:

\[
x-2=\frac12(2x-1)-\frac32,
\qquad\text{since }Q'=2x-1 .
\]

Hence  

\[
\int\frac{x-2}{Q}\,dx
=\frac12\int\frac{2x-1}{Q}\,dx-\frac32\int\frac{dx}{Q}
=\frac12\ln Q-\frac32\int\frac{dx}{(x-\tfrac12)^2+\bigl(\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\bigr)^2}.
\]

The last integral is elementary:

\[
\int\frac{dx}{(x-\tfrac12)^2+(\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2})^{2}}
=\frac{2}{\sqrt3}\arctan\!\left(\frac{2x-1}{\sqrt3}\right).
\]

Collecting everything,

\[
\begin{aligned}
\int\ln (x^{2}-x+1)\,dx
&=x\ln Q-\Bigl[2x+\frac12\ln Q-\sqrt3\arctan\!\Bigl(\frac{2x-1}{\sqrt3}\Bigr)\Bigr]+C\\[4pt]
&=\bigl(x-\tfrac12\bigr)\ln (x^{2}-x+1)-2x
+\sqrt3\arctan\!\Bigl(\frac{2x-1}{\sqrt3}\Bigr)+C .
\end{aligned}
\]

\[
\boxed{\displaystyle 
\int \ln (x^{2}-x+1)\,dx=
\left(x-\frac12\right)\!\ln (x^{2}-x+1)-2x
+\sqrt3\,\arctan\!\left(\frac{2x-1}{\sqrt3}\right)+C }
\]
It seems simple, but I'm unsure about the details: Solve the equation $\cos 3x\cos^3 x+\sin 3x\sin^3 x=0.$

First the conclusion, then the reasoning: \[
\cos 3x\cos ^3x+\sin 3x\sin ^3x=0 ,\qquad x\in\mathbb R
\]

---

### 1.  Write everything with \(\sin x,\cos x\)

\[
\cos 3x = 4\cos ^3x-3\cos x ,\qquad 
\sin 3x = 3\sin x-4\sin ^3x .
\]

Put \(c=\cos x,\;s=\sin x\;(c^2+s^2=1)\):

\[
(4c^{3}-3c)c^{3}+(3s-4s^{3})s^{3}=0
\]

\[
4c^{6}-3c^{4}+3s^{4}-4s^{6}=0 .
\]

---

### 2.  Factor

\[
\begin{aligned}
4c^{6}-4s^{6}-3c^{4}+3s^{4}
&=4(c^{6}-s^{6})-3(c^{4}-s^{4})\\[2mm]
&=4(c^{2}-s^{2})(c^{4}+c^{2}s^{2}+s^{4})
   -3(c^{2}-s^{2})(c^{2}+s^{2}) .
\end{aligned}
\]

Since \(c^{2}+s^{2}=1\),

\[
(c^{2}-s^{2})\Bigl[\,4(c^{4}+c^{2}s^{2}+s^{4})-3\,\Bigr]=0 .
\]

Thus we have two possible factors.

---

### 3.  First factor  

\[
c^{2}-s^{2}=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\cos 2x=0 .
\]

Hence  

\[

x=\frac{\pi}{4}+k\frac{\pi}{2},\qquad k\in\mathbb Z .
\]

\[
4(c^{4}+c^{2}s^{2}+s^{4})-3=0 .
\]

Because \(c^{2}+s^{2}=1\),

\[
c^{4}+c^{2}s^{2}+s^{4}= (c^{2}+s^{2})^{2}-c^{2}s^{2}=1-c^{2}s^{2}.
\]

Hence  

\[
4(1-c^{2}s^{2})=3\quad\Longrightarrow\quad c^{2}s^{2}=\frac14 .
\]

But \(c^{2}s^{2}= \sin^{2}x\cos^{2}x =\frac{\sin^{2}2x}{4}\); therefore  

\[
\frac{\sin^{2}2x}{4}= \frac14\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \sin^{2}2x=1
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \sin 2x=\pm1 .
\]

Thus  

\[
2x=\frac{\pi}{2}+k\pi\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
x=\frac{\pi}{4}+k\frac{\pi}{2},\qquad k\in\mathbb Z .
\]

---

### 5.  Solution set

Both factors give the same set of angles, so the complete solution of  

\[
\cos 3x\cos ^3x+\sin 3x\sin ^3x=0
\]

is  

\[
\boxed{\,x=\frac{\pi}{4}+k\frac{\pi}{2},\qquad k\in\mathbb Z\,}.
\]

(Any integer \(k\) yields a valid real solution; the equation is periodic with period \(\pi\).)
What would be a clean way to solve this? Find the smallest $\lambda > 0$ such that $u \le v + \log(u+1)$ implies $u \le v + \lambda + \log(v+1)$.

Here's the core idea and its execution: Let  

\[
u\le v+\log (u+1)\qquad (\ast )
\]

and we want a constant \(\lambda>0\) such that  

\[
u\le v+\lambda+\log (v+1)\qquad (\dagger )
\]

holds for **all** real numbers \(u,v\) for which \((\ast )\) is true.  
For a fixed pair \((u,v)\) satisfying \((\ast )\),

\[
u-v-\log (v+1)\le \lambda .
\]

Hence the smallest admissible \(\lambda\) is the supremum of the left‑hand side over the region defined by \((\ast )\):

\[
\boxed{\;\lambda_{\min}= \sup_{u,v\;:\;u\le v+\log (u+1)}
\bigl[u-v-\log (v+1)\bigr]\;}
\tag{1}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  Reduce to a single variable  

From \((\ast )\) we have \(v\ge u-\log (u+1)\).  
Since the expression in (1) decreases when \(v\) increases, the supremum is attained at the smallest admissible \(v\), i.e. at  

\[
v=u-\log (u+1).
\]

Insert this into the quantity to be maximised:

\[
\begin{aligned}
u-v-\log (v+1)
&=u-\bigl(u-\log (u+1)\bigr)-\log\!\bigl(u-\log (u+1)+1\bigr)\\[2mm]
&=\log (u+1)-\log\!\bigl(u-\log (u+1)+1\bigr).
\end{aligned}
\]

Thus define  

\[
\phi(u)=\log\frac{u+1}{\,u-\log (u+1)+1\,},
\qquad u>-1,
\]

and \(\lambda_{\min}= \displaystyle\sup_{u>-1}\phi(u)\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  A convenient change of variable  

Put \(x=u+1\;(>0)\). Then \(u=x-1\) and  

\[
\phi(u)=\log\frac{x}{x-\log x}
      =-\log\!\Bigl(1-\frac{\log x}{x}\Bigr).
\]

Hence  

\[
\lambda_{\min}= \sup_{x>0}\Bigl\{-\log\!\Bigl(1-\frac{\log x}{x}\Bigr)\Bigr\}.
\tag{2}
\]

The function \(-\log(1-y)\) is increasing in \(y\) for \(0<y<1\); therefore the supremum in (2) is attained when the ratio  

\[
y(x)=\frac{\log x}{x}
\]

is maximal.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Maximising \(\displaystyle y(x)=\frac{\log x}{x}\)

\[
y'(x)=\frac{1-\log x}{x^{2}}.
\]

\(y'(x)=0\) gives \(\log x=1\), i.e. \(x=e\).  
For \(0<x<e\), \(y'(x)>0\); for \(x>e\), \(y'(x)<0\).  
Thus \(x=e\) yields the global maximum

\[
y_{\max}=y(e)=\frac{\log e}{e}= \frac{1}{e}.
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4.  The supremum value  

Insert \(y_{\max}=1/e\) into (2):

\[
\lambda_{\min}= -\log\!\Bigl(1-\frac{1}{e}\Bigr)
               = -\log\!\Bigl(\frac{e-1}{e}\Bigr)
               = \log\frac{e}{e-1}.
\]

Equivalently,

\[
\boxed{\displaystyle \lambda_{\min}=1-\log(e-1)}.
\]

Numerically,

\[
\lambda_{\min}= \log\frac{e}{e-1}\approx 0.458676.
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 5.  Verification that the bound is attainable  

At the maximizing point \(x=e\) (i.e. \(u=e-1\)) we have  

\[
v=u-\log(u+1)= (e-1)-\log e = e-2,
\]

which satisfies \(v>-1\) and indeed

\[
u = v+\log(u+1),\qquad 
u = v+\lambda_{\min}+\log(v+1).
\]

Thus the constant cannot be reduced any further.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
**Answer:**  

\[
\boxed{\displaystyle \lambda_{\min}= \log\frac{e}{e-1}=1-\log(e-1)\approx 0.4587 }.
\]

Could you help me make sense of this problem? A smaller square was cut out of a larger square such that one of the sides of the smaller square lies on the side of the larger square. The perimeter of the resulting octagon is 40% larger than the perimeter of the original square. By what percentage is the area of the resulting octagon less than the area of the original square?

Alright, here's a step-by-step explanation: Let the side of the original square be \(L\) and let the side of the cut‑out square be \(x\).

---

### 1.  Perimeter of the octagon  

When the small square is cut out so that one of its sides lies on a side of the large square, the side of the large square is broken into three pieces:

* a left segment,
* the side of the small square (length \(x\)) which is removed,
* a right segment.

The three other sides of the small square become part of the new perimeter.  
Hence the new perimeter is  

\[
\text{new perimeter}=4L - x + 3x = 4L + 2x .
\]

We are told that this perimeter is \(40\%\) larger than the original perimeter \(4L\):

\[
4L + 2x = 1.40\,(4L)=5.6L .
\]

Solving for \(x\),

\[
2x = 5.6L-4L = 1.6L \quad\Longrightarrow\quad x = 0.8L .
\]

---

### 2.  Area of the octagon  

The original area is \(L^{2}\).  
The area removed (the small square) is \(x^{2} = (0.8L)^{2}=0.64L^{2}\).

Therefore the area of the resulting octagon is  

\[
\text{remaining area}=L^{2}-0.64L^{2}=0.36L^{2}.
\]

---

### 3.  Percentage decrease in area  

\[
\frac{\text{area removed}}{\text{original area}}=
\frac{0.64L^{2}}{L^{2}} = 0.64 = 64\%.
\]

Thus the area of the octagon is **64 % less** than the area of the original square.
Can you outline a strategy for this question? Solve the following logarithmic equations. $\log _{x+1}(x^2+x-6)^2=4$.

Sure, let's start with the idea: \[
\log_{x+1}\bigl(x^{2}+x-6\bigr)^{2}=4
\]

---

### 1.  Domain conditions  

* Base of a logarithm must be positive and different from \(1\):
  \[
  x+1>0,\qquad x+1\neq 1\Longrightarrow x>-1,\;x\neq 0 .
  \]

* The argument must be positive:
  \[
  \bigl(x^{2}+x-6\bigr)^{2}>0\Longrightarrow x^{2}+x-6\neq 0 .
  \]

Thus we will keep only the solutions that satisfy  

\[
x>-1,\;x\neq 0,\;x\neq -3,\;x\neq 2 .
\]

---

### 2.  Remove the logarithm  

\[
\log_{x+1}\bigl(x^{2}+x-6\bigr)^{2}=4
\Longrightarrow (x+1)^{4}= \bigl(x^{2}+x-6\bigr)^{2}.
\]

Both sides are non‑negative, so we can take square roots:

\[
|(x+1)^{2}| = \bigl|x^{2}+x-6\bigr|.
\]

Since \((x+1)^{2}\ge 0\), the absolute value disappears on the left:

\[
(x+1)^{2}=|x^{2}+x-6|.
\]

Hence we have two possibilities.

---

### 3.  Solve the two cases  

#### **Case A:** \((x+1)^{2}=x^{2}+x-6\)

\[
x^{2}+2x+1 = x^{2}+x-6\quad\Longrightarrow\quad 2x+1 = x-6
\]
\[
x = -7.
\]

But \(x=-7\) gives a base \(x+1=-6<0\); a logarithm cannot have a negative base.  
\(\Rightarrow\) discard.

---

#### **Case B:** \((x+1)^{2}=-(x^{2}+x-6)\)

\[
x^{2}+2x+1 = -x^{2}-x+6
\]
\[
2x^{2}+3x-5 = 0.
\]

Solve the quadratic:

\[
\Delta = 3^{2}-4\cdot2(-5)=9+40=49,\qquad \sqrt\Delta =7,
\]
\[
x=\frac{-3\pm7}{2\cdot2}= \frac{-3\pm7}{4}.
\]

Thus  

\[
x_{1}= \frac{4}{4}=1,\qquad x_{2}= \frac{-10}{4}= -\frac52 .
\]

Check the domain:

* \(x=1\): \(x+1=2>0\) and \(x\neq0,-3,2\). Accept.
* \(x=-\dfrac52\): \(x+1=-\dfrac32<0\). Reject (base not positive).

---

### 4.  Verification  

For \(x=1\):
\[
\log_{1+1}\bigl(1^{2}+1-6\bigr)^{2}= \log_{2}(-4)^{2}= \log_{2}16 =4,
\]
which satisfies the original equation.

---

## Solution

\[
\boxed{x=1}
\]

How would you approach this? How many operations can be conducted at least to guarantee the identification of at least $10$ genuine coins if there are $31$ metal coins that look identical, among which $28$ are genuine and $3$ are fake? The genuine coins have the same weight among themselves, and the fake coins also have the same weight among themselves, but the fake coins are lighter than the genuine ones. In each operation, the coins are placed on the pans of a balance to be weighed, and it is determined which pan has a greater total weight or if the weights on both pans are equal.

Let's outline the key steps: **Answer: one weighing is enough (and of course at least one weighing is necessary).**

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### Why one weighing suffices  

Take any 11 coins and put them on the left pan, take another 11 (different) coins and put them on the right pan; the remaining 9 coins are left aside.  
Let  

* \(a\) = number of fake (lighter) coins among the 11 on the left,  
* \(b\) = number of fake coins among the 11 on the right.  

Because there are only three fakes,  

\[
a+b\le 3 .
\]

The balance can give three possible results.

| Result of the balance | Relation between \(a\) and \(b\) | Possibilities for \((a,b)\) | Max. number of fakes on the indicated side |
|------------------------|-----------------------------------|-----------------------------|--------------------------------------------|
| **Left heavier**      | \(a<b\)                           | \((0,1),(0,2),(0,3),(1,2)\) | at most **1** fake on the left |
| **Right heavier**     | \(b<a\)                           | symmetric to the left case | at most **1** fake on the right |
| **Balance**           | \(a=b\)                           | \((0,0)\) or \((1,1)\)      | at most **1** fake on each side |

In every case the side that is **heavier** (or either side when the scale balances) contains **at most one fake coin**.  
Since each side holds 11 coins, that side must contain at least  

\[
11-1 = 10
\]

genuine (heavy) coins.

Thus after a single weighing we can point to the 11 coins on the heavier pan (or to any pan when the scale balances) and be certain that at least ten of them are genuine.

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### Why we cannot do it with zero weighings  

Without any weighing we have no information about which of the 31 coins are light.  
Choosing any particular set of ten coins could, in the worst‑case arrangement of the three fakes, contain a fake coin. Hence we cannot guarantee ten genuine coins without performing at least one weighing.

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### Minimal number of operations  

Consequently the smallest number of balance‑operations that guarantees the identification of at least ten genuine coins is  

\[
\boxed{1}.
\]
Starting from basics, how should I solve this? Find the function \( f(x) \) such that \( f(x) = \cos(2mx) + \int_{0}^{\pi} f(t) |\cos t| \, dt \) for a positive integer \( m \).

Alright, here's a step-by-step explanation: \[
f(x)=\cos (2mx)+\int_{0}^{\pi}f(t)\,|\cos t|\,dt ,\qquad m\in \mathbb N .
\]

The integral on the right–hand side does not depend on \(x\); denote it by a constant \(C\):

\[
f(x)=\cos (2mx)+C ,\qquad 
C=\int_{0}^{\pi}f(t)\,|\cos t|\,dt .
\]

Insert \(f(t)=\cos (2mt)+C\) into the definition of \(C\):

\[
\begin{aligned}
C&=\int_{0}^{\pi}\bigl[\cos (2mt)+C\bigr]|\cos t|\,dt   \\
  &=\underbrace{\int_{0}^{\pi}\cos (2mt)|\cos t|\,dt}_{I_m}
    +C\underbrace{\int_{0}^{\pi}|\cos t|\,dt}_{A}.
\end{aligned}
\]

---

### 1.  The integral \(A\)

\[
A=\int_{0}^{\pi}|\cos t|\,dt
   =\int_{0}^{\pi/2}\cos t\,dt+\int_{\pi/2}^{\pi}(-\cos t)\,dt
   =1+1=2 .
\]

Hence  

\[
C=I_m+2C\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad C=-I_m .
\]

---

### 2.  Computing \(I_m\)

Because \(|\cos t|=\operatorname{sgn}(\cos t)\cos t\),

\[
I_m=\int_{0}^{\pi}\cos (2mt)\,|\cos t|\,dt
    =\int_{0}^{\pi/2}\cos (2mt)\cos t\,dt
      -\int_{\pi/2}^{\pi}\cos (2mt)\cos t\,dt .
\]

Use \(\cos a\cos b=\tfrac12[\cos(a+b)+\cos(a-b)]\):

\[
\cos (2mt)\cos t=\frac12\bigl[\cos((2m+1)t)+\cos((2m-1)t)\bigr].
\]

Thus  

\[
\begin{aligned}
I_m&=\frac12\Bigl[
      \int_{0}^{\pi/2}\!\!\bigl(\cos((2m+1)t)+\cos((2m-1)t)\bigr)dt
     -\int_{\pi/2}^{\pi}\!\!\bigl(\cos((2m+1)t)+\cos((2m-1)t)\bigr)dt
     \Bigr] \\[2mm]
   &=\frac12\bigl[J_{2m+1}+J_{2m-1}\bigr],
\end{aligned}
\]

where  

\[
J_k=\int_{0}^{\pi/2}\cos(kt)\,dt-\int_{\pi/2}^{\pi}\cos(kt)\,dt
    =\frac{2\sin(k\pi/2)}{k}.
\]

Hence  

\[
I_m=\frac{\sin\bigl((2m+1)\frac{\pi}{2}\bigr)}{2m+1}
     +\frac{\sin\bigl((2m-1)\frac{\pi}{2}\bigr)}{2m-1}.
\]

For an integer \(m\),

\[
\sin\!\Bigl((2m+1)\frac{\pi}{2}\Bigr)=(-1)^{m},\qquad
\sin\!\Bigl((2m-1)\frac{\pi}{2}\Bigr)=(-1)^{m-1}.
\]

Therefore  

\[
\begin{aligned}
I_m&=(-1)^{m}\frac{1}{2m+1}+(-1)^{m-1}\frac{1}{2m-1}\\
   &=(-1)^{m}\Bigl(\frac{1}{2m+1}-\frac{1}{2m-1}\Bigr)\\[2mm]
   &=(-1)^{m+1}\frac{2}{(2m-1)(2m+1)} .
\end{aligned}
\]

---

### 3.  The constant \(C\)

Since \(C=-I_m\),

\[
C=\frac{2(-1)^{m}}{(2m-1)(2m+1)} .
\]

---

### 4.  The function \(f\)

Finally  

\[
\boxed{\displaystyle 
f(x)=\cos(2mx)+\frac{2(-1)^{m}}{(2m-1)(2m+1)}},
\qquad m=1,2,3,\dots
\]

One may verify directly that this \(f\) satisfies  

\[
f(x)=\cos(2mx)+\int_{0}^{\pi}f(t)\,|\cos t|\,dt .
\]

I tried a few ideas but failed. What's the right approach? Evaluate the integral $\int \frac{\sqrt{\cos x}}{\sin x} \, dx$.

A concise solution goes like this: \[
I=\int\frac{\sqrt{\cos x}}{\sin x}\,dx
\]

---

### 1.  Substitution  

Put  

\[
t=\sqrt{\cos x}\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad t^{2}= \cos x .
\]

Differentiating,
\[
2t\,dt = -\sin x\,dx\quad\Longrightarrow\quad dx=-\frac{2t}{\sin x}\,dt .
\]

Hence  

\[
\frac{\sqrt{\cos x}}{\sin x}\,dx
   =\frac{t}{\sin x}\Bigl(-\frac{2t}{\sin x}\,dt\Bigr)
   =-\,\frac{2t^{2}}{\sin^{2}x}\,dt .
\]

Because \(\sin^{2}x=1-\cos^{2}x=1-t^{4}\),

\[
I=-2\int\frac{t^{2}}{1-t^{4}}\,dt .
\]

---

### 2.  Partial‑fraction decomposition  

\[
\frac{t^{2}}{1-t^{4}}
   =\frac{t^{2}}{(1-t^{2})(1+t^{2})}
   =\frac{1/2}{1-t^{2}}-\frac{1/2}{1+t^{2}} .
\]

Therefore  

\[
I=-2\int\Bigl[\frac{1/2}{1-t^{2}}-\frac{1/2}{1+t^{2}}\Bigr]dt
   =-\int\frac{dt}{1-t^{2}}+\int\frac{dt}{1+t^{2}} .
\]

---

### 3.  Integrate  

\[
\int\frac{dt}{1+t^{2}} = \arctan t + C .
\]

For the other term, write  

\[
\frac{1}{1-t^{2}}=\frac12\Bigl(\frac{1}{1-t}+\frac{1}{1+t}\Bigr),
\]

so  

\[
\int\frac{dt}{1-t^{2}}
   =\frac12\Bigl[-\ln|1-t|+\ln|1+t|\Bigr]
   =\frac12\ln\Bigl|\frac{1+t}{1-t}\Bigr|
   =\operatorname{arctanh} t .
\]

Thus  

\[
I= -\operatorname{arctanh} t + \arctan t + C .
\]

---

### 4.  Return to \(x\)

Recall \(t=\sqrt{\cos x}\).  Hence

\[
\boxed{\displaystyle 
\int\frac{\sqrt{\cos x}}{\sin x}\,dx
   =\arctan\!\bigl(\sqrt{\cos x}\bigr)
    -\operatorname{arctanh}\!\bigl(\sqrt{\cos x}\bigr)
    +C } .
\]

Equivalently, using the logarithmic form of \(\operatorname{arctanh}\),

\[
\int\frac{\sqrt{\cos x}}{\sin x}\,dx
   =\arctan\!\bigl(\sqrt{\cos x}\bigr)
    -\frac12\ln\Bigl|\frac{1+\sqrt{\cos x}}{1-\sqrt{\cos x}}\Bigr|
    +C .
\]

Before I overcomplicate it, what's the key insight? Given a quadrilateral \(ABCD\) and a point \(M\) that runs along \(AB\) (excluding \(A\) and \(B\)), two circles \((MAC)\) and \((MBD)\) intersect at points \(M\) and \(N\). Find the locus of point \(N\).

We can break it down as follows: Let  

\[
M\in AB\;(M\neq A,B),\qquad 
\omega _1=(MAC),\qquad 
\omega _2=(MBD)
\]

and let  

\[
\omega _1\cap\omega _2=\{M,N\}.
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  \(N\) is the centre of a spiral similarity  

Because \(A,C,M,N\) are concyclic, the oriented angles satisfy  

\[
\angle ANM=\angle ACM .\tag{1}
\]

Because \(B,D,M,N\) are concyclic, we also have  

\[
\angle BNM=\angle BDM .\tag{2}
\]

From (1) and (2)

\[
\angle ANM=\angle ACM,\qquad 
\angle BNM=\angle BDM .
\]

Hence the directed angles  

\[
\angle ANB=\angle ACM+\angle BDM=\angle ACB+\angle BDA .
\]

Thus the transformation that sends the segment \(AC\) to the segment \(BD\) is a
rotation‑dilation (a **spiral similarity**) whose centre is the point \(N\):
it sends \(A\mapsto B\) and \(C\mapsto D\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  The centre of a spiral similarity sending \(AC\) to \(BD\) lies on \(CD\)

Let \(S\) be the centre of a spiral similarity that carries the segment
\(AC\) onto the segment \(BD\).  
The similarity sends the line \(AC\) onto the line \(BD\); therefore it sends
the point \(C\) to the point \(D\).  Consequently the points \(C\), \(D\) and
the centre \(S\) are collinear (the image of a point under a spiral similarity
lies on the line joining the point with the centre).  
Hence every centre of a spiral similarity that maps \(AC\) onto \(BD\) belongs
to the line \(CD\).

Applying this to the point \(N\) found above, we obtain  

\[
N\in CD .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  The locus of \(N\)

For each position of \(M\) on the side \(AB\) the circles \((MAC)\) and
\((MBD)\) intersect again at a point \(N\) that is the centre of the spiral
similarity sending \(AC\) to \(BD\); therefore \(N\) always lies on the line
\(CD\).

Conversely, for any point \(N\) on the line \(CD\) (different from \(C\) and
\(D\)) there exists a unique point \(M\in AB\) such that the circles
\((MAC)\) and \((MBD)\) meet again at \(N\) (the required \(M\) is the
intersection of the line \(AB\) with the line through \(N\) that is the image
of \(AB\) under the same spiral similarity).  Hence every point of the line
\(CD\) is attained.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
\[
\boxed{\text{The locus of the second intersection }N\text{ is the (extended)
line }CD.}
\]

Thus, as the point \(M\) slides along the side \(AB\) of the quadrilateral,
the point \(N\) slides along the opposite side \(CD\).  (If \(C\) and \(D\)
coincide, the locus degenerates to that single point.)

It seems simple, but I'm unsure about the details: Find a polynomial \( f(x) \) of degree 3 such that the remainder when \( f(x) \) is divided by \( x-2 \) is 8 and the remainder when \( f(x) \) is divided by \( x-3 \) is -5.

Alright, here's a step-by-step explanation: Let  

\[
f(x)=ax^{3}+bx^{2}+cx+d ,\qquad a\neq 0
\]

and use the given remainder conditions.

---

### 1.  Translate the remainder conditions  

When a polynomial is divided by \(x-2\) the remainder is the value at \(x=2\); similarly for \(x-3\).  
Hence  

\[
f(2)=8,\qquad f(3)=-5 .
\]

---

### 2.  Write \(f(x)\) in a convenient form  

Factor out the product \((x-2)(x-3)\) (which vanishes at the two points) and add a linear term that will supply the required values:

\[
f(x)=(x-2)(x-3)q(x)+\bigl(mx+n\bigr),
\]

where \(q(x)\) is any polynomial and \(mx+n\) is the remainder when dividing by \((x-2)(x-3)\).  
Because we need a cubic polynomial, we can take \(q(x)\) to be linear:
\(q(x)=kx+\ell\) with \(k\neq 0\).

---

### 3.  Determine the linear remainder  

We require  

\[
\begin{cases}
mx+n = f(2)=8,\\[2pt]
mx+n = f(3)=-5 .
\end{cases}
\]

Thus  

\[
\begin{aligned}
2m+n &= 8,\\
3m+n &= -5 .
\end{aligned}
\]

Subtracting gives \(m=-13\); then \(n = 8-2(-13)=34\).

Hence the linear part is \(-13x+34\).

---

### 4.  Choose a simple \(q(x)\)  

Take the simplest non‑zero linear polynomial, \(q(x)=x\) (i.e. \(k=1,\ \ell=0\)).  

Now  

\[
\begin{aligned}
f(x) &= (x-2)(x-3)\,x \;+\;(-13x+34)\\
     &= x\bigl(x^{2}-5x+6\bigr)-13x+34\\
     &= x^{3}-5x^{2}+6x-13x+34\\
     &= x^{3}-5x^{2}-7x+34 .
\end{aligned}
\]

---

### 5.  Verify  

\[
\begin{aligned}
f(2) &= 2^{3}-5\cdot2^{2}-7\cdot2+34 = 8-20-14+34 = 8,\\
f(3) &= 3^{3}-5\cdot3^{2}-7\cdot3+34 = 27-45-21+34 = -5.
\end{aligned}
\]

Both conditions are satisfied, and the degree of \(f\) is 3.

---

\[
\boxed{\,f(x)=x^{3}-5x^{2}-7x+34\,}
\]

(Any other cubic obtained by choosing a different linear \(q(x)\) would also work; the above is a convenient example.)

Can you outline a strategy for this question? A rectangular area of 9000 m$^2$ must be surrounded by a fence, with two opposite sides being made of brick and the other two of wood. One meter of wooden fencing costs 10 roubles while one meter of brick walling costs 25 roubles. What is the least amount of money that must be allotted to the construction of such a fence?

First the conclusion, then the reasoning: Let  

\[
x,\;y>0\qquad\text{be the side lengths of the rectangle (metres).}
\]

The area condition is  

\[
xy = 9000\;\text{m}^2 .\tag{1}
\]

Two opposite sides are built of brick, the other two of wood.  
The price per metre is  

* brick : \(25\) roubles,

Starting from basics, how should I solve this? Find the largest number that is a multiple of 3 and cannot be written as \(7a + 11b\), where \(a\) and \(b\) are positive integers.

Here's a clear solution: Let  

\[
N=7a+11b ,\qquad a,b\in \mathbb Z_{>0}.
\]

Since both \(a\) and \(b\) must be at least \(1\), write  

\[
a=1+x,\qquad b=1+y\qquad (x,y\ge 0).
\]

Then  

\[
N = 7(1+x)+11(1+y)=18+7x+11y .
\]

Hence a number \(N\) can be written as \(7a+11b\) with \(a,b>0\) **iff**  

\[
N-18 = 7x+11y\qquad (x,y\ge 0).
\]

So we have to find the largest multiple of \(3\) for which \(N-18\) is **not** a non‑negative combination of \(7\) and \(11\).

---

### 1.  Frobenius number for \(\{7,11\}\)

Because \(\gcd(7,11)=1\), the largest integer that cannot be expressed as a non‑negative combination of \(7\) and \(11\) is  

\[
g = 7\cdot 11-7-11 = 59 .
\]

Thus every integer \(>59\) can be written as \(7x+11y\) with \(x,y\ge 0\).

Consequently, if  

\[
N-18 > 59\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad N>77,
\]

then \(N-18\) is representable, and therefore \(N\) **is** representable with \(a,b>0\).

Hence any counter‑example must satisfy  

\[
N\le 77 .
\]

Since we are interested only in multiples of \(3\), we need only check the multiples of \(3\) up to \(75\) (the largest multiple of \(3\) not exceeding \(77\)).

---

### 2.  Which numbers \(\le 75\) fail?

List the numbers that are **not** representable as \(7x+11y\) for \(x,y\ge 0\) up to \(57\) (because \(N-18\le 75-18=57\)):

\[
\begin{aligned}
&1,2,3,4,5,6,8,9,10,12,13,15,16,17,\\
&19,20,23,24,26,27,30,31,34,37,38,41,45,48,52 .
\end{aligned}
\]

Add \(18\) to each of these to obtain the corresponding \(N\):

\[
\begin{aligned}
&19,20,21,22,23,24,26,27,28,30,31,33,34,35,\\
&37,38,41,42,44,45,48,49,52,55,56,59,63,66,70 .
\end{aligned}
\]

Now keep only the multiples of \(3\):

\[
21,\;24,\;27,\;30,\;33,\;42,\;45,\;48,\;63,\;66 .
\]

These are exactly the multiples of \(3\) \(\le 75\) that **cannot** be written as \(7a+11b\) with \(a,b>0\).

---

### 3.  The largest one

The largest element of the above list is  

\[
\boxed{66}.
\]

---

### 4.  Verification

Assume \(66 = 7a+11b\) with \(a,b\ge 1\).  
Subtract \(18\):

\[
66-18 = 48 = 7(a-1)+11(b-1),
\]

where \(a-1,b-1\ge 0\).  
Trying all possibilities for \(b-1 = y =0,1,2,3,4\) gives

\[
\begin{array}{c|c}
y & 48-11y \\
\hline
0 & 48 \\
1 & 37 \\
2 & 26 \\
3 & 15 \\
4 & 4
\end{array}
\]

None of these remainders is a multiple of \(7\); hence no non‑negative integer \(x\) satisfies \(7x+11y=48\).  
Thus no positive integers \(a,b\) exist, confirming that \(66\) indeed cannot be expressed in the required form.

Since every larger multiple of \(3\) (i.e., \(69,72,75\)) does admit such a representation, \(66\) is the largest possible.
