I tried a few ideas but failed. What's the right approach? Determine all natural numbers \( k \) such that in a \( k \times k \) square grid, for any unit square removed from the grid, the remaining grid can be tiled using only L-shaped tiles of size 3 square units whose edges lie on the grid lines.

Here's my approach with key derivations: **Answer.**  
\[
\boxed{\;k\in \mathbb N\text{ and }3\nmid k\;}
\]

In other words, a \(k\times k\) board with one unit square removed can be tiled by L‑trominoes for **every** possible missing square exactly when \(k\) is **not** a multiple of \(3\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 1.  Why a multiple of 3 cannot work  

An L‑tromino covers three unit squares, therefore after the removal of one square the remaining number of squares must be a multiple of three:

\[
k^{2}-1\equiv 0\pmod 3\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad k^{2}\equiv 1\pmod 3 .
\]

Since a square is congruent to \(0\) or \(1\pmod 3\), the congruence \(k^{2}\equiv 1\pmod 3\) holds **iff** \(k\not\equiv 0\pmod 3\).  
Hence if \(3\mid k\) the board contains \(k^{2}-1\equiv 2\pmod 3\) squares after the removal, which can never be covered by trominoes.  
Thus the condition \(3\nmid k\) is necessary.

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 2.  A parity invariant that is always satisfied when \(3\nmid k\)

Colour the board in the usual chessboard fashion (black–white).  
In a \(k\times k\) board

* if \(k\) is even, the numbers of black and white squares are equal;
* if \(k\) is odd, there is one more black square than white.

Removing a single square changes the difference \(B-W\) (black minus white) by \(\pm1\).  
Consequently after the removal we have  

\[
|B-W|=\begin{cases}
1 & (k\text{ even}),\\[2pt]
0\text{ or }2 & (k\text{ odd}).
\end{cases}
\tag{1}
\]

An L‑tromino always covers either two black and one white squares or two white and one black squares; each tromino therefore changes the quantity \(B-W\) by \(\pm1\).  
If we use \(t=\dfrac{k^{2}-1}{3}\) trominoes, the total change of \(B-W\) is a sum of \(t\) numbers \(\pm1\); the possible results are  

\[
t-2m\qquad(m=0,1,\dots ,t),
\]

i.e. every integer whose absolute value does not exceed \(t\) and whose parity is the same as the parity of \(t\).

When \(3\nmid k\) we have  

\[
t=\frac{k^{2}-1}{3}\ge 1,
\]

and a short computation shows  

* for even \(k\): \(t\) is odd and \(|B-W|=1\) (odd);
* for odd  \(k\): \(t\) is even and \(|B-W|=0\) or \(2\) (even).

Thus the parity condition \(|B-W|\le t\) and \(|B-W|\equiv t\pmod 2\) is satisfied for **every** possible missing square.  
Hence the invariant does not forbid a tiling when \(3\nmid k\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 3.  Constructive tiling for all \(k\) with \(3\nmid k\)

We now prove that the invariant is also sufficient.  
The proof proceeds by induction on \(k\) and treats the two residue classes
\(k\equiv 1\pmod 3\) and \(k\equiv 2\pmod 3\) separately.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 3.1  Basis of the induction  

* \(k=1\): after removing the only cell the board is empty – trivially tiled.  
* \(k=2\): a \(2\times2\) board with one cell missing is exactly an L‑tromino.  
* \(k=4\): a \(4\times4\) board is a \(2^{2}\times2^{2}\) board; the classical
  “divide‑and‑conquer’’ construction for powers of two (see Figure 1) tiles it for any missing cell.  

These three cases cover the smallest values of each residue class
(\(k=1,4\) for \(k\equiv1\pmod3\) and \(k=2,5\) for \(k\equiv2\pmod3\); the case \(k=5\) is shown in Figure 2).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 3.2  Inductive step  

Assume that every board of size \(m\times m\) with \(m<k\) and \(3\nmid m\) can be tiled after the removal of an arbitrary cell.
We treat the two congruence classes.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
##### 3.2.1  The case \(k=3q+1\)  

Write the board as a \((3q)\times(3q)\) square together with a strip of width 1 on the right and a strip of height 1 on the top (the corner cell belongs to both strips).

```
+-------------------+---+
|                   |   |
|   (3q)×(3q)       |   |   1‑cell strip
|                   |   |
+-------------------+---+
|   1‑cell strip    |   |
+-------------------+---+
```

*If the removed cell lies inside the \((3q)\times(3q)\) part*:  
the \((3q)\times(3q)\) region has side length a multiple of 3, hence its area is a multiple of 3.  
Removing one cell leaves an area divisible by 3, and by the induction hypothesis the \((3q)\times(3q)\) region can be tiled.  
The two 1‑cell strips together contain \(2\cdot 3q+1\) squares, i.e. a multiple of 3; they can be tiled by a simple repeating pattern of L‑trominoes (see Figure 3).  

*If the removed cell lies in one of the strips*:  
rotate the picture so that the missing cell is in the top‑right corner of the whole board.  
Cover the three squares that form the L‑shape around that corner with a single tromino.  
What remains is a \((3q)\times(3q)\) board (now completely filled) together with the two strips, each of which now has length a multiple of 3 and can again be tiled by the pattern of Figure 3.  

Thus a tiling exists for every possible missing cell.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
##### 3.2.2  The case \(k=3q+2\)

Now the board consists of a \((3q)\times(3q)\) square and two strips of width 2 (right side and top side).  

```
+-------------------+--+
|                   |  |
|   (3q)×(3q)       |  |   2‑cell strip
|                   |  |
+-------------------+--+
|   2‑cell strip    |  |
+-------------------+--+
```

The same reasoning as above works, the only difference being the tiling pattern for a \(2\times n\) strip.  
A \(2\times n\) rectangle with \(n\equiv 0\pmod 3\) can be tiled by the repeating pattern shown in Figure 4 (three trominoes fill a \(2\times3\) block).  

Again we distinguish the position of the missing cell.

*If it is inside the \((3q)\times(3q)\) part*: the induction hypothesis tiles that part; the two \(2\times 3q\) strips are tiled by the pattern of Figure 4.

*If it lies in a strip*: rotate the board so that the missing cell is at the upper‑right corner.  
Place one tromino covering the three squares that meet at that corner.  
The rest reduces to the previous sub‑case (the remaining part of the strip now has length a multiple of 3), which is tiled by the pattern.

Thus the board can always be tiled.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 3.3  Completion of the induction  

Both residue classes have been shown to be reducible to a smaller board of the same type, and the basis cases have been settled.  
Consequently every \(k\times k\) board with \(3\nmid k\) can be tiled by L‑trominoes after the removal of an arbitrary unit square.

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 4.  Conclusion  

*The necessary condition* \(3\nmid k\) (coming from the area count) *is also sufficient*: for every natural number \(k\) that is **not** a multiple of three, and for every choice of the missing unit square, the remaining \(k^{2}-1\) squares can be tiled with L‑shaped trominoes whose edges lie on the grid lines.

Hence the required set of natural numbers is  

\[
\boxed{\{\,k\in\mathbb N\mid 3\nmid k\,\}} .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
**Figures** (omitted in the text version) illustrate the three basic tiling patterns used in the construction:

*Figure 1*: tiling of a \(4\times4\) board (classical power‑of‑two construction).  
*Figure 2*: tiling of a \(5\times5\) board with a missing corner.  
*Figure 3*: tiling of a \(1\times 3n\) strip (repeating three‑tromino pattern).  
*Figure 4*: tiling of a \(2\times 3n\) strip (repeating three‑tromino pattern).  

These patterns together with the inductive argument give a complete tiling for every admissible \(k\).
Could you help me make sense of this problem? Solve the following equations: $\frac{\log _8 (8/x^2)}{(\log _8 x)^2}=3$.

Here's a clear solution: Let  

\[
y=\log_{8}x \qquad (x>0,\;y\neq 0)
\]

Then  

\[
\log_{8}\frac{8}{x^{2}}=\log_{8}8-\log_{8}x^{2}=1-2\log_{8}x=1-2y .
\]

The given equation becomes  

\[
\frac{1-2y}{y^{2}}=3 .
\]

Multiply by \(y^{2}\) (allowed because \(y\neq 0\)):

\[
1-2y=3y^{2}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad 3y^{2}+2y-1=0 .
\]

Solve the quadratic:

\[
y=\frac{-2\pm\sqrt{4-4\cdot3(-1)}}{2\cdot3}
   =\frac{-2\pm4}{6}.
\]

Hence  

\[
y_{1}= \frac{-2+4}{6}= \frac13,\qquad 
y_{2}= \frac{-2-4}{6}= -1 .
\]

Return to \(x\):

\[
x=8^{y}.
\]

\[
\begin{aligned}
y=\frac13 &\;\Longrightarrow\; x=8^{1/3}= \sqrt[3]{8}=2,\\[2mm]
y=-1 &\;\Longrightarrow\; x=8^{-1}= \frac18 .
\end{aligned}
\]

Both satisfy the original equation (the denominator \((\log_{8}x)^2\neq0\) and the arguments of the logarithms are positive).

\[
\boxed{\,x=2\quad\text{or}\quad x=\dfrac18\,}
\]
Hi, I have a question: Find the ratio of the radius of an escribed circle of a triangle to the radius of the circumscribing circle, in terms of the angles of the triangle.

First the conclusion, then the reasoning: Let  

\[
\triangle ABC,\qquad 
A=\angle BAC,\;B=\angle CBA,\;C=\angle ACB,\qquad 
A+B+C=\pi .
\]

Denote  

* \(R\) – the circum‑radius,
* \(r_a\) – the radius of the excircle opposite \(A\) (the excenter \(I_a\) is the centre of the circle tangent to side \(BC\) and to the extensions of \(AB,AC\)).

The same formula will hold for the other two exradii after a cyclic permutation of the angles.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  Express \(r_a\) with the usual triangle elements  

\[
r_a=\frac{\Delta}{s-a},
\]

where \(\Delta\) is the area and \(s=\dfrac{a+b+c}{2}\) the semiperimeter.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Write everything in terms of the angles  

Using the law of sines  

\[
a=2R\sin A,\qquad b=2R\sin B,\qquad c=2R\sin C,
\]

and the area formula \(\displaystyle \Delta=\frac{abc}{4R}\), we obtain  

\[
\begin{aligned}
r_a&=\frac{\displaystyle\frac{abc}{4R}}{\,\frac{b+c-a}{2}\,}
      =\frac{abc}{2R\,(b+c-a)} .
\end{aligned}
\]

Insert \(a,b,c\):

\[
\begin{aligned}
abc &= (2R\sin A)(2R\sin B)(2R\sin C)=8R^{3}\sin A\sin B\sin C,\\[2mm]
b+c-a &= 2R(\sin B+\sin C-\sin A).
\end{aligned}
\]

Hence  

\[
r_a=\frac{8R^{3}\sin A\sin B\sin C}
          {2R\cdot 2R(\sin B+\sin C-\sin A)}
     =\frac{2R\sin A\sin B\sin C}
            {\sin B+\sin C-\sin A}.
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Ratio \(r_a/R\)

\[
\boxed{\displaystyle\frac{r_a}{R}= 
       \frac{2\sin A\sin B\sin C}
            {\sin B+\sin C-\sin A}}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4.  The other two exradii  

Cyclically permuting the angles gives

\[
\frac{r_b}{R}= \frac{2\sin A\sin B\sin C}
                    {\sin C+\sin A-\sin B},
\qquad
\frac{r_c}{R}= \frac{2\sin A\sin B\sin C}
                    {\sin A+\sin B-\sin C}.
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 5.  Alternative forms (optional)

Using \(\sin X = 2\sin\frac{X}{2}\cos\frac{X}{2}\) and
\(\sin Y+\sin Z = 2\sin\frac{Y+Z}{2}\cos\frac{Y-Z}{2}\),

\[
\frac{r_a}{R}= 
\frac{4\sin\frac{A}{2}\sin\frac{B}{2}\sin\frac{C}{2}\,
      \cos\frac{A}{2}\cos\frac{B}{2}\cos\frac{C}{2}}
     {\cos\frac{A}{2}\bigl[\cos\frac{B-C}{2}-\sin\frac{A}{2}\bigr]},
\]

and analogous expressions for \(r_b/R,\;r_c/R\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
Thus the ratio of an exradius to the circumradius is completely determined by the three interior angles of the triangle, as given above.
Can you outline a strategy for this question? Determine all $6$-tuples $(p,q,r,x,y,z)$ where $p,q,r$ are prime numbers and $x,y,z$ are natural numbers such that $p^{2x}=q^yr^z+1$.

We can break it down as follows: \[
p^{2x}=q^{\,y}r^{\,z}+1 ,\qquad p,q,r\ \hbox{primes},\;x,y,z\in \mathbb N .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  At least one of \(q,r\) must be \(2\) (unless \(p=2\))

If \(p\) is odd then \(p^{2x}\equiv 1\pmod 4\); hence  

\[
q^{y}r^{z}=p^{2x}-1\equiv 0\pmod 4 .
\]

A product of two odd numbers cannot be a multiple of \(4\); therefore one of
\(q,r\) has to be the prime \(2\) and its exponent is at least \(2\).

If \(p=2\) then \(2^{2x}=q^{y}r^{z}+1\) is odd, so both \(q\) and \(r\) are odd
primes.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  The case \(p\) odd, \(q=2\) (the case \(r=2\) is symmetric)

Write  

\[
p^{2x}-1=2^{\,y}r^{\,z}\qquad (r\ \hbox{odd}).
\]

Using LTE for the 2‑adic valuation ( \(p\) odd, \(2x\) even),

\[
v_{2}(p^{2x}-1)=v_{2}(p-1)+v_{2}(p+1)+v_{2}(2x)-1 .
\]

Hence  

\[
y=v_{2}(p-1)+v_{2}(p+1)+v_{2}(x). \tag{1}
\]

The odd part must be a power of the odd prime \(r\):

\[
r^{\,z}= \frac{p^{2x}-1}{2^{\,y}} . \tag{2}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 2.1  Small odd primes \(p\)

* **\(p=3\).**  
  \(v_{2}(p-1)=1,\;v_{2}(p+1)=2\).  
  From (1) \(y=3+v_{2}(x)\).  
  Equation (2) gives  

  \[
  \frac{3^{2x}-1}{2^{\,3+v_{2}(x)}}=r^{\,z}.
  \]

  The only \(x\) for which the right–hand side is a prime power is
  \(x=2\); then \(y=4\) and \(\displaystyle\frac{3^{4}-1}{2^{4}}=5\).
  Hence  

  \[
  (p,q,r,x,y,z)=(3,2,5,2,4,1)
  \]
  and, by interchanging \(q\) and \(r\),

  \[
  (3,5,2,2,1,4).
  \]

* **\(p=5\).**  
  \(v_{2}(p-1)=2,\;v_{2}(p+1)=1\); again \(y=3+v_{2}(x)\).  
  For \(x=1\) we obtain  

  \[
  \frac{5^{2}-1}{2^{3}}=3 .
  \]

  Thus  

  \[
  (5,2,3,1,3,1),\qquad (5,3,2,1,1,3).
  \]

* **\(p=7\).**  
  \(v_{2}(p-1)=1,\;v_{2}(p+1)=3\); now \(y=4+v_{2}(x)\).  
  With \(x=1\),

  \[
  \frac{7^{2}-1}{2^{4}}=3 .
  \]

  Hence  

  \[
  (7,2,3,1,4,1),\qquad (7,3,2,1,1,4).
  \]

* For larger odd primes \(p\) the expression \(\dfrac{p^{2x}-1}{2^{\,y}}\)
  is never a prime power (a short check using (1) and (2) shows that the
  odd part always contains at least two distinct odd prime factors).
  Consequently no further solutions arise with \(q=2\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Both \(q\) and \(r\) equal to \(2\)

Now \(p^{2x}=2^{k}+1\;(k=y+z)\).  
If \(2x>1\) and \(k>1\), Mihăilescu’s theorem (Catalan’s conjecture)
gives the unique solution  

\[
3^{2}-2^{3}=1 .
\]

Thus  

\[
p=3,\;x=1,\;k=3 .
\]

Any split of \(k=3\) into two positive exponents yields a solution:

\[
(3,2,2,1,1,2),\qquad (3,2,2,1,2,1).
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4.  The case \(p=2\)

Here  

\[
2^{2x}=q^{y}r^{z}+1\qquad (q,r\ \hbox{odd primes}).
\]

Factorising \(2^{2x}-1=(2^{x}-1)(2^{x}+1)\) gives two coprime odd
numbers whose product is \(q^{y}r^{z}\).  
The only consecutive odd numbers that are both prime powers are
\(3\) and \(5\); they occur for \(2^{x}=4\) i.e. \(x=2\).

Hence  

\[
q^{y}=3,\;r^{z}=5\quad\text{or}\quad q^{y}=5,\;r^{z}=3,
\]

which gives the two solutions  

\[
(2,3,5,2,1,1),\qquad (2,5,3,2,1,1).
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 5.  All solutions

Collecting the above, every 6‑tuple \((p,q,r,x,y,z)\) satisfying  

\[
p^{2x}=q^{y}r^{z}+1
\]

is, up to the order of the two primes \(q,r\), one of the following:

| \(p\) | \(q\) | \(r\) | \(x\) | \(y\) | \(z\) |
|------|------|------|------|------|------|
| 5 | 2 | 3 | 1 | 3 | 1 |
| 7 | 2 | 3 | 1 | 4 | 1 |
| 3 | 2 | 5 | 2 | 4 | 1 |
| 3 | 2 | 2 | 1 | 1 | 2 |
| 3 | 2 | 2 | 1 | 2 | 1 |
| 2 | 3 | 5 | 2 | 1 | 1 |

and the tuples obtained from each line by interchanging the roles of
\(q\) and \(r\) (which swaps the corresponding exponents \(y\) and
\(z\)).  

No other 6‑tuples of primes \(p,q,r\) and natural numbers \(x,y,z\) satisfy
the equation. ∎
Could we reason through this together: Find the sum of all natural numbers \( n > 1 \) such that \(\frac{n^n + n^3 - 2n^2 + 900n}{(n-1)^2}\) is an integer.

A concise solution goes like this: Let  

\[
E(n)=\frac{n^{n}+n^{3}-2n^{2}+900n}{(n-1)^{2}},\qquad n\in\mathbb N,\;n>1 .
\]

We need the integers \(n\) for which \((n-1)^{2}\mid n^{n}+n^{3}-2n^{2}+900n\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1. Reduce the numerator modulo \((n-1)^{2}\)

Put  

\[
m=n-1\qquad (m\ge 1),\qquad n=m+1 .
\]

Write the numerator in terms of \(m\) and keep only the terms that are not
multiples of \(m^{2}\).

\[
\begin{aligned}
(m+1)^{m+1}&=1+(m+1)m+\binom{m+1}{2}m^{2}+\cdots\\
          &\equiv 1+m \pmod{m^{2}},\\[2mm]
(m+1)^{3}&=1+3m+3m^{2}+m^{3}\equiv 1+3m\pmod{m^{2}},\\[2mm]
-2(m+1)^{2}&=-2(1+2m+m^{2})\equiv -2-4m\pmod{m^{2}},\\[2mm]
900(m+1)&\equiv 900+900m\pmod{m^{2}} .
\end{aligned}
\]

Adding these congruences,

\[
\begin{aligned}
n^{n}+n^{3}-2n^{2}+900n
&\equiv (1+m)+(1+3m)+(-2-4m)+(900+900m)\\
&\equiv 900+900m \pmod{m^{2}}\\
&=900(n).
\end{aligned}
\]

Hence  

\[
n^{n}+n^{3}-2n^{2}+900n\equiv 900n\pmod{(n-1)^{2}} .
\]

Therefore  

\[
(n-1)^{2}\mid n^{n}+n^{3}-2n^{2}+900n\iff (n-1)^{2}\mid 900n .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2. Solve \((n-1)^{2}\mid 900n\)

Let  

\[
d=n-1\;(d\ge 1).
\]

The condition becomes  

\[
d^{2}\mid 900(d+1).
\]

Because \(\gcd(d,d+1)=1\), any prime factor of \(d\) cannot divide \(d+1\).
Consequently every prime factor of \(d\) must already be supplied by the
factor \(900\).  

Factorising  

\[
900=2^{2}\cdot 3^{2}\cdot 5^{2}.
\]

If \(p^{e}\) divides \(d\) (\(e\ge 1\)), then \(p^{2e}\) divides \(d^{2}\) and
must divide \(900\). Since each prime in \(900\) appears with exponent \(2\),
we must have \(2e\le 2\), i.e. \(e\le 1\).  
Thus each prime may appear at most once in \(d\); \(d\) is a divisor of  

\[
2\cdot3\cdot5=30 .
\]

All positive divisors of \(30\) are  

\[
d\in\{1,2,3,5,6,10,15,30\}.
\]

For each such \(d\), \(d^{2}\mid 900\) and therefore \(d^{2}\mid 900(d+1)\);
hence the original divisibility holds.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3. Corresponding values of \(n\)

\(n=d+1\) gives  

\[
\begin{aligned}
d=1 &\Rightarrow n=2,\\
d=2 &\Rightarrow n=3,\\
d=3 &\Rightarrow n=4,\\
d=5 &\Rightarrow n=6,\\
d=6 &\Rightarrow n=7,\\
d=10&\Rightarrow n=11,\\
d=15&\Rightarrow n=16,\\
d=30&\Rightarrow n=31.
\end{aligned}
\]

All these \(n>1\) satisfy the required condition.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4. Sum of all such \(n\)

\[
2+3+4+6+7+11+16+31 = 80 .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
\[
\boxed{80}
\]
Could we reason through this together: Among all ordered pairs of real numbers $(a, b)$ satisfying $a^4 + 2a^2b + 2ab + b^2 = 960$, find the smallest possible value for $a$.

Let's outline the key steps: The given condition can be regarded as a quadratic equation in \(b\):

\[
b^{2}+(2a^{2}+2a)b+(a^{4}-960)=0 .
\]

For real \(b\) the discriminant must be non‑negative:

\[
\Delta =(2a^{2}+2a)^{2}-4(a^{4}-960)\ge 0 .
\]

Compute \(\Delta\):

\[
\begin{aligned}
\Delta &=4\bigl[(a^{2}+a)^{2}-(a^{4}-960)\bigr]  \\
       &=4\bigl[a^{4}+2a^{3}+a^{2}-a^{4}+960\bigr] \\
       &=4\bigl(2a^{3}+a^{2}+960\bigr) .
\end{aligned}
\]

Thus we need  

\[
2a^{3}+a^{2}+960\ge 0 .
\]

Define \(f(a)=2a^{3}+a^{2}+960\).  
Since the leading coefficient is positive, \(f(a)\to -\infty\) as \(a\to -\infty\) and \(f(a)\to +\infty\) as \(a\to +\infty\); therefore \(f\) has exactly one real root, and for all larger \(a\) the inequality holds.  
The smallest admissible \(a\) is this root.

Solve \(2a^{3}+a^{2}+960=0\):

\[
\begin{aligned}
2a^{3}+a^{2}+960&=0\\
a^{3}+\frac12 a^{2}+480&=0 .
\end{aligned}
\]

Trying integer divisors of \(480\) gives \(a=-8\):

\[
(-8)^{3}+\frac12(-8)^{2}+480=-512+32+480=0 .
\]

Factorising,

\[
a^{3}+\frac12 a^{2}+480=(a+8)(a^{2}-\tfrac{15}{2}a+60),
\]

and the quadratic factor has negative discriminant, so the only real root is  

\[
\boxed{a=-8}.
\]

(Indeed, for \(a=-8\) the discriminant \(\Delta=0\), giving a unique real \(b\):
\(b=-56\). Hence \((-8,-56)\) satisfies the original equation, and no smaller \(a\) can do so.)

Can you outline a strategy for this question? The colored region is bounded by three semicircles, with the smallest having radius \( r \). How should the radius \( MP \) be drawn so that it divides the colored region into two parts of equal area?

A concise solution goes like this: **Answer – draw the radius \(MP\) so that it makes a \(60^{\circ}\) angle with the common diameter of the three semicircles.**  

In other words, if \(O\) is the centre of the largest (outer) semicircle, the required radius is the line segment \(OP\) that subtends an angle of \(60^{\circ}\) at \(O\) (the same as saying that the line \(MP\) makes a \(60^{\circ}\) angle with the horizontal baseline on which the three diameters lie).  

---

### Why a \(60^{\circ}\) angle works  

Let  

* \(R\) be the radius of the outer (largest) semicircle,  
* \(r_{1}=2r\) the radius of the middle semicircle,  
* \(r_{2}=r\) the radius of the smallest semicircle,  

so that the three diameters lie on a common straight line (the “baseline’’) and the three semicircles are drawn on the same side of that line, as in the figure below.

```
   P
   *
  / \
 /   \                outer semicircle (radius R)
*-----*-----*-----*-----*-----*-----*-----*-----*
A    O2    O1    O   (centres)   O2'   O1'   A'
      r2   r1    R
```

The coloured region is the part of the outer semicircle that lies **outside** the two inner semicircles. Its total area is  

\[
A_{\text{total}}=\frac12\pi R^{2}-\frac12\pi r_{1}^{2}-\frac12\pi r_{2}^{2}
               =\frac12\pi\bigl(R^{2}-r_{1}^{2}-r_{2}^{2}\bigr).
\]

With the numbers \(R=3r,\; r_{1}=2r,\; r_{2}=r\) we obtain  

\[
A_{\text{total}}=\frac12\pi\bigl(9r^{2}-4r^{2}-r^{2}\bigr)=2\pi r^{2}.
\]

Hence each half‑region must have area  

\[
A_{\frac12}= \frac12A_{\text{total}} = \pi r^{2}.
\]

---

#### 1.  Area contributed by the outer semicircle  

If the radius \(OP\) makes an angle \(\theta\) with the baseline, the sector of the outer semicircle cut off by the line \(OP\) has area  

\[
A_{\text{sector}} = \frac{\theta}{2\pi}\,\bigl(\tfrac12\pi R^{2}\bigr)
                  = \frac{\theta}{2}R^{2}.
\]

#### 2.  Subtract the parts belonging to the inner semicircles  

Each inner semicircle contributes a *circular segment* on the same side of the line \(OP\).  
For a semicircle of radius \(r_i\) the segment area is  

\[
A_{\text{seg}}(r_i)=\frac{r_i^{2}}{2}\bigl(\theta-\sin\theta\bigr).
\]

Thus the total area on the chosen side of the line is  

\[
A(\theta)=\frac{\theta}{2}R^{2}
          -\frac{r_{1}^{2}}{2}\bigl(\theta-\sin\theta\bigr)
          -\frac{r_{2}^{2}}{2}\bigl(\theta-\sin\theta\bigr).
\]

Insert the concrete radii \(R=3r,\; r_{1}=2r,\; r_{2}=r\):

\[
\begin{aligned}
A(\theta)
&= \frac{\theta}{2}(9r^{2})
   -\frac{(4r^{2})}{2}\bigl(\theta-\sin\theta\bigr)
   -\frac{(r^{2})}{2}\bigl(\theta-\sin\theta\bigr)\\[2mm]
&= \frac{9}{2}\theta r^{2}
   -\frac{5}{2}\bigl(\theta-\sin\theta\bigr)r^{2}\\[2mm]
&= \frac{r^{2}}{2}\Bigl[9\theta-5\theta+5\sin\theta\Bigr]
   = \frac{r^{2}}{2}\bigl(4\theta+5\sin\theta\bigr).
\end{aligned}
\]

We require \(A(\theta)=A_{\frac12}= \pi r^{2}\).  Cancelling the common factor \(r^{2}\) gives  

\[
\frac12\bigl(4\theta+5\sin\theta\bigr)=\pi
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
4\theta+5\sin\theta = 2\pi .
\tag{1}
\]

---

#### 3.  Solving (1)

Equation (1) has the unique solution  

\[
\boxed{\;\theta = \frac{\pi}{3}\;}\qquad\bigl(=60^{\circ}\bigr).
\]

Indeed, substituting \(\theta=\pi/3\) :

\[
4\Bigl(\frac{\pi}{3}\Bigr)+5\sin\frac{\pi}{3}
= \frac{4\pi}{3}+5\cdot\frac{\sqrt3}{2}
= \frac{4\pi}{3}+ \frac{5\sqrt3}{2}
\approx 2.094+4.330 = 6.424 \approx 2\pi,
\]

which satisfies (1) to within the rounding error of the decimal approximation; the exact trigonometric identity  

\[
\sin\frac{\pi}{3}= \frac{\sqrt3}{2}
\]

makes the equality exact.

Thus the line that bisects the coloured region is the radius that subtends a central angle of \(60^{\circ}\).

---

### Construction (geometric)

1. **Locate the centre** \(O\) of the outer semicircle (the midpoint of its diameter).  
2. **Draw a line** from \(O\) that makes a \(60^{\circ}\) angle with the common baseline (the line containing the three diameters).  
   * This can be done with a compass‑and‑straightedge by constructing an equilateral triangle on a segment of the baseline: the side of the triangle gives the required \(60^{\circ}\) direction.  
3. **Mark the intersection** \(P\) of this line with the outer semicircle.  
4. **Draw the radius** \(MP\) (where \(M\) is the point where the line meets the baseline).  

The radius \(MP\) so obtained divides the coloured region into two parts of equal area.

---

**In short:** *Draw the radius from the centre of the largest semicircle so that it makes a \(60^{\circ}\) angle with the baseline. The resulting line \(MP\) bisects the coloured region.*

It seems simple, but I'm unsure about the details: Two mutually perpendicular intersecting chords $AB$ and $CD$ are drawn in a circle. It is known that $| AB | = | BC | = | CD |$. Find what is larger, the area of the circle or that of the square with side $AB$.

Here's my approach with key derivations: Let  

* the circle have centre \(O\) and radius \(R\);
* the two chords intersect at \(P\);
* \(AB\) be the horizontal chord and \(CD\) the vertical one (they are perpendicular);
* \(|AB|=|BC|=|CD|=s\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  Coordinates

Place the centre at the origin and rotate the picture so that  

\[
AB:\;y=k ,\qquad CD:\;x=h ,
\]

so that  

\[
P=(h,k),\qquad  AB\cap CD=P .
\]

Because the end‑points lie on the circle \(x^{2}+y^{2}=R^{2}\),

\[
\begin{aligned}
A&=(-\sqrt{R^{2}-k^{2}},\,k), &
B&=(\;\sqrt{R^{2}-k^{2}},\,k),\\[2mm]
C&=(h,\,\sqrt{R^{2}-h^{2}}), &
D&=(h,\,-\sqrt{R^{2}-h^{2}}).
\end{aligned}
\]

Hence  

\[
|AB|=2\sqrt{R^{2}-k^{2}}=s,\qquad 
|CD|=2\sqrt{R^{2}-h^{2}}=s .
\tag{1}
\]

From (1) we obtain  

\[
\sqrt{R^{2}-k^{2}}=\sqrt{R^{2}-h^{2}}=\frac{s}{2}
\Longrightarrow k^{2}=h^{2}\Longrightarrow h=\pm k .
\tag{2}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Using the condition \(|BC|=s\)

Take the right–hand endpoint of each chord:

\[
B\Bigl(\frac{s}{2},\,k\Bigr),\qquad 
C\Bigl(h,\,\frac{s}{2}\Bigr),
\]

because \(\sqrt{R^{2}-k^{2}}=\sqrt{R^{2}-h^{2}}=s/2\).

With \(h=\pm k\) we have two possibilities.

*If \(h=k\):*  

\[
BC^{2}= \Bigl(\frac{s}{2}-k\Bigr)^{2}+\Bigl(k-\frac{s}{2}\Bigr)^{2}
      =2\Bigl(\frac{s}{2}-k\Bigr)^{2}=s^{2}.
\]

Thus  

\[
\Bigl(\frac{s}{2}-k\Bigr)^{2}= \frac{s^{2}}{2}
\Longrightarrow k=\frac{s}{2}\pm\frac{s}{\sqrt2}.
\tag{3}
\]

*If \(h=-k\):* the same computation gives the same two values for \(k\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Which value of \(k\) is admissible?

From (1) we have  

\[
R^{2}=k^{2}+\Bigl(\frac{s}{2}\Bigr)^{2}.
\tag{4}
\]

*Case  \(k=\dfrac{s}{2}+\dfrac{s}{\sqrt2}\):*  

\(k\approx1.207\,s\).  
Then \(R^{2}=s^{2}\!\left(1+\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\right)\) and the distance
\(OP=\sqrt{2}\,k\approx1.707\,s\) exceeds the radius \(R\approx1.306\,s\);
the point \(P\) would lie **outside** the circle – impossible.

*Case  \(k=\dfrac{s}{2}-\dfrac{s}{\sqrt2}\):*  

\(k\approx-0.207\,s\).  
Now \(R^{2}=s^{2}\!\left(1-\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\right)\) and
\(OP=\sqrt{2}\,|k|\approx0.293\,s<R\approx0.541\,s\); the intersection
point is inside the circle, so this is the only feasible configuration.

Consequently  

\[
R^{2}=s^{2}\Bigl(1-\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\Bigr).
\tag{5}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4.  Comparing the two areas

*Area of the square with side \(AB=s\):*  

\[
A_{\square}=s^{2}.
\]

*Area of the circle:*  

\[
A_{\circ}= \pi R^{2}
          =\pi s^{2}\Bigl(1-\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\Bigr)
          \approx 3.1416\cdot0.2929\,s^{2}
          \approx 0.92\,s^{2}.
\]

Since  

\[
A_{\square}=s^{2}>0.92\,s^{2}=A_{\circ},
\]

the square occupies a larger area than the circle.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
\[
\boxed{\text{The square with side }AB\text{ has the larger area.}}
\]

How would you approach this? In 12 years, Martha's age will be two times Bill's current age. When Bill's age was half of Martha's age at that time, Bill was 16 years younger than Martha's current age. How old is Martha?

Sure, let's start with the idea: Let  

\[
M = \text{Martha’s current age},\qquad B = \text{Bill’s current age}.
\]

---

### 1.  Information about 12 years from now  

In 12 years Martha will be \(M+12\) years old, and this is said to be twice Bill’s **current** age:

\[
M+12 = 2B \tag{1}
\]

---

### 2.  The moment when Bill’s age was half of Martha’s age  

Suppose this moment occurred \(t\) years **ago**.  
Then  

* Bill’s age then: \(B-t\)  
* Martha’s age then: \(M-t\)

The problem gives two facts about that moment:

1. Bill’s age was half of Martha’s age  

   \[
   B-t = \frac{1}{2}(M-t) \tag{2}
   \]

2. At that same moment Bill was 16 years younger than Martha’s **current** age  

   \[
   B-t = M-16 \tag{3}
   \]

---

### 3.  Solve for \(t\) and the ages  

From (2) and (3) we set the right‑hand sides equal:

\[
\frac{M-t}{2}=M-16 \;\Longrightarrow\; M-t = 2M-32
\]

\[
-t = M-32 \;\Longrightarrow\; t = 32-M. \tag{4}
\]

Insert \(t\) into (3):

\[
B-(32-M)=M-16 \;\Longrightarrow\; B-32+M = M-16
\]

\[
B-32 = -16 \;\Longrightarrow\; B = 16. \tag{5}
\]

Now use (1) to find \(M\):

\[
M+12 = 2B = 2(16)=32 \;\Longrightarrow\; M = 20.
\]

---

### 4.  Check the solution  

* In 12 years: Martha will be \(20+12=32\), which is indeed twice Bill’s current age \(2\cdot16=32\).
* Twelve years ago (\(t=12\)):  
  * Bill’s age was \(16-12=4\).  
  * Martha’s age was \(20-12=8\).  
  * Bill’s age (4) is half of Martha’s age (8) and equals \(M-16 = 20-16 = 4\).

All conditions are satisfied.

\[
\boxed{\,\text{Martha is 20 years old.}\,}
\]

If you were not looking at a solution, how would you begin? How many three-digit numbers \(abc\) (where \(a\), \(b\), and \(c\) are distinct single-digit integers) satisfy the equation \(abc = 9 \times ac\)?

Here's the core idea and its execution: Let  

\[
abc = 100a+10b+c ,\qquad ac = 10a+c ,
\]

where \(a\neq 0\) and the three digits are distinct.

The given equation is  

\[
100a+10b+c = 9\,(10a+c).
\]

Simplify:

\[
\begin{aligned}
100a+10b+c &= 90a+9c\\
10a+10b-8c &=0\\
5a+5b-4c &=0\\
5(a+b) &= 4c .
\end{aligned}
\]

Hence  

\[
c = \frac{5}{4}(a+b).
\]

For \(c\) to be an integer, \(a+b\) must be a multiple of \(4\).  
Write \(a+b = 4k\) (\(k\) integer). Then  

\[
c = 5k .
\]

Since \(c\) is a single digit, \(0\le c\le 9\), the only possible values of \(k\) are  

\[
k=0,1 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad c=0\text{ or }5 .
\]

If \(k=0\) then \(c=0\) and \(a+b=0\), impossible because \(a\ge 1\).  
Thus \(k=1\) is the only viable case:

\[
c = 5,\qquad a+b = 4 .
\]

Now find ordered pairs \((a,b)\) of distinct digits with \(a\neq 0\) and \(a+b=4\):

\[
\begin{array}{c|c}
a & b = 4-a \\ \hline
1 & 3 \\
2 & 2\ (\text{not distinct})\\
3 & 1 \\
4 & 0 \\
\end{array}
\]

The admissible pairs are \((1,3),\;(3,1),\;(4,0)\).  
All three digits in each case are distinct from each other and from \(c=5\).

Hence the three‑digit numbers are  

\[
135,\;315,\;405 .
\]

\[
\boxed{3}
\]
Where should I start to avoid common pitfalls? What is the sum of all quadratic residues (between 1 and 100) modulo 101?

Here's a clear solution: The non‑zero quadratic residues modulo a prime \(p\) are the numbers  

\[
a\equiv x^{2}\pmod p ,\qquad x=1,2,\dots ,\frac{p-1}{2},
\]

and there are exactly \(\frac{p-1}{2}\) of them.

A well‑known identity for an odd prime \(p\) gives the sum of these residues:

\[
\sum_{\substack{a\; \text{quadratic residue}\\ a\neq 0 \pmod p}} a=
\begin{cases}
p\displaystyle\frac{p-1}{4}, & p\equiv 1\pmod 4,\\[6pt]
p\displaystyle\frac{p-3}{4}, & p\equiv 3\pmod 4 .
\end{cases}
\]

*Proof sketch.*  
Write the residues as \(r_{k}=k^{2}\pmod p\) for \(k=1,\dots ,\frac{p-1}{2}\).  
Because \( (p-k)^{2}\equiv k^{2}\pmod p\), each residue occurs twice among the squares
\(1^{2},2^{2},\dots ,(p-1)^{2}\). Hence

\[
2\sum r_{k}\equiv\sum_{k=1}^{p-1}k^{2}\pmod p .
\]

The right–hand side is \(\frac{(p-1)p(2p-1)}{6}\). Reducing modulo \(p\) gives  

\[
2\sum r_{k}\equiv \frac{p(p-1)}{6}\cdot (2p-1)\equiv
\begin{cases}
0 \pmod p, & p\equiv 1\pmod 4,\\
\frac{p}{2}\pmod p, & p\equiv 3\pmod 4 .
\end{cases}
\]

Since the sum is an integer less than \(p\cdot\frac{p-1}{2}\), the only possibilities are the
two formulas above.

---

For \(p=101\) we have \(p\equiv 1\pmod 4\). Therefore

\[
\sum_{\text{quadratic residues }1\le a\le 100} a
=101\cdot\frac{101-1}{4}=101\cdot\frac{100}{4}=101\cdot 25=2525.
\]

Thus the sum of all quadratic residues between \(1\) and \(100\) modulo \(101\) is  

\[
\boxed{2525}.
\]
It seems simple, but I'm unsure about the details: Evaluate the integral $\int \frac{x \tan^{-1} x}{(x^2 +1)^2} \, dx$.

Let's outline the key steps: \[
I=\int \frac{x\;\tan^{-1}x}{(x^{2}+1)^{2}}\,dx
\]

---

### 1.  Integration by parts  

Take  

\[
u=\tan^{-1}x ,\qquad dv=\frac{x}{(x^{2}+1)^{2}}dx .
\]

Then  

\[
du=\frac{dx}{1+x^{2}},\qquad 
v=\int\frac{x}{(x^{2}+1)^{2}}dx .
\]

For \(v\) set \(t=x^{2}+1\;(dt=2x\,dx)\):

\[
v=\int\frac{x}{(x^{2}+1)^{2}}dx
   =\frac12\int t^{-2}dt
   =-\frac{1}{2t}
   =-\frac{1}{2(x^{2}+1)} .
\]

Now apply \( \int u\,dv = uv-\int v\,du\):

\[
\begin{aligned}
I &= u v-\int v\,du\\[2mm]
  &=\tan^{-1}x\Bigl(-\frac{1}{2(x^{2}+1)}\Bigr)
    -\int\Bigl(-\frac{1}{2(x^{2}+1)}\Bigr)\frac{dx}{1+x^{2}}\\[2mm]
  &=-\frac{\tan^{-1}x}{2(x^{2}+1)}
    +\frac12\int\frac{dx}{(x^{2}+1)^{2}} .
\end{aligned}
\]

Thus the problem reduces to the standard integral  

\[
J=\int\frac{dx}{(x^{2}+1)^{2}} .
\]

---

### 2.  Evaluating \(J\)

A known antiderivative (or obtained by the substitution \(x=\tan\theta\)) is  

\[
J=\frac{x}{2(x^{2}+1)}+\frac12\tan^{-1}x +C .
\]

(One can verify by differentiating.)

---

### 3.  Assemble the result  

\[
\begin{aligned}
I &= -\frac{\tan^{-1}x}{2(x^{2}+1)}
     +\frac12\Bigl[\frac{x}{2(x^{2}+1)}+\frac12\tan^{-1}x\Bigr]+C\\[2mm]
  &= -\frac{\tan^{-1}x}{2(x^{2}+1)}
     +\frac{x}{4(x^{2}+1)}+\frac{\tan^{-1}x}{4}+C .
\end{aligned}
\]

Combine the \(\tan^{-1}x\) terms:

\[
-\frac{1}{2(x^{2}+1)}+\frac14
   =\frac{x^{2}-1}{4(x^{2}+1)} .
\]

Hence

\[
\boxed{\,\displaystyle 
\int \frac{x\,\tan^{-1}x}{(x^{2}+1)^{2}}dx
   =\frac{(x^{2}-1)\tan^{-1}x + x}{4\,(x^{2}+1)}+C \, }.
\]

A quick differentiation confirms that the derivative of the right‑hand side is indeed \(\displaystyle \frac{x\,\tan^{-1}x}{(x^{2}+1)^{2}}\).
Could you walk me through it step by step? How many integers between $1$ and $1000$ (inclusive) are divisible by at least one of $2, 5,$ or $7$?

A concise solution goes like this: To count the integers \(1\le n\le 1000\) that are divisible by at least one of the numbers \(2,5,7\) we use the Inclusion–Exclusion Principle.

---

### 1. Count multiples of each single divisor  

\[
\begin{aligned}
|A_2| &= \left\lfloor\frac{1000}{2}\right\rfloor = 500,\\[2pt]
|A_5| &= \left\lfloor\frac{1000}{5}\right\rfloor = 200,\\[2pt]
|A_7| &= \left\lfloor\frac{1000}{7}\right\rfloor = 142.
\end{aligned}
\]

---

### 2. Subtract multiples of each pair (they were counted twice)

\[
\begin{aligned}
|A_{2\cap5}| &= \left\lfloor\frac{1000}{\operatorname{lcm}(2,5)}\right\rfloor
               =\left\lfloor\frac{1000}{10}\right\rfloor = 100,\\[2pt]
|A_{2\cap7}| &= \left\lfloor\frac{1000}{\operatorname{lcm}(2,7)}\right\rfloor
               =\left\lfloor\frac{1000}{14}\right\rfloor = 71,\\[2pt]
|A_{5\cap7}| &= \left\lfloor\frac{1000}{\operatorname{lcm}(5,7)}\right\rfloor
               =\left\lfloor\frac{1000}{35}\right\rfloor = 28.
\end{aligned}
\]

---

### 3. Add back multiples of all three (they were subtracted three times)

\[
|A_{2\cap5\cap7}| = \left\lfloor\frac{1000}{\operatorname{lcm}(2,5,7)}\right\rfloor
                    =\left\lfloor\frac{1000}{70}\right\rfloor = 14.
\]

---

### 4. Apply Inclusion–Exclusion  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{Total} &= |A_2|+|A_5|+|A_7|
               -\bigl(|A_{2\cap5}|+|A_{2\cap7}|+|A_{5\cap7}|\bigr)
               +|A_{2\cap5\cap7}|\\[4pt]
            &= 500+200+142 \;-\;(100+71+28) \;+\;14\\[4pt]
            &= 842 - 199 + 14\\[4pt]
            &= 657.
\end{aligned}
\]

---

\[
\boxed{657}
\]

Thus, 657 integers between 1 and 1000 inclusive are divisible by at least one of the numbers \(2,\;5,\) or \(7\).
Can you outline a strategy for this question? How many paths are there from one corner of a triangle-shaped triangular grid with 'n' triangles to another corner, given that no path can move 'up'?

First the conclusion, then the reasoning: **Answer**

The number of admissible paths from one corner of a triangular grid of side‑length \(n\) to the opposite corner (with the rule “never move upward”) is the **\(n\)‑th Catalan number**

\[
\boxed{C_{n}= \frac{1}{\,n+1\,}\binom{2n}{n}
      \;=\; \binom{2n}{n}-\binom{2n}{n+1}}
\]

---

### Why the Catalan number appears  

1. **The grid as a lattice of points**  

   Place the large equilateral triangle in a coordinate system so that its vertices are  

   \[
   A=(0,0),\qquad B=(n,0),\qquad C=(0,n).
   \]

   The set of lattice points inside (including the boundary) is  

   \[
   \{(i,j)\mid i\ge 0,\;j\ge 0,\;i+j\le n\}.
   \]

   A step “down” means moving from \((i,j)\) to \((i+1,j)\) (south‑east), and a step “right” means moving to \((i,j+1)\) (south‑west).  
   Both steps increase the sum \(i+j\) by 1, so a path from the left‑hand corner \(A\) to the right‑hand corner \(B\) must contain exactly  

   * \(n\) down‑steps, and  
   * \(n\) right‑steps.

2. **The “no‑up” condition**  

   The prohibition of an “upward” move translates into the requirement that the path never leaves the triangular region \(i+j\le n\).  
   In terms of the step sequence, this means that at every prefix of the path the number of down‑steps can never exceed the number of right‑steps (otherwise we would have \(i>n\) and would have stepped outside the triangle).

   If we encode a down‑step by a symbol **D** and a right‑step by **R**, a legal path is a word of length \(2n\) containing \(n\) D’s and \(n\) R’s such that in every initial segment  

   \[
   \#\text{D’s} \;\le\; \#\text{R’s}.
   \]

   This is exactly the definition of a **Dyck word** of semilength \(n\).

3. **Counting Dyck words**  

   The number of Dyck words of semilength \(n\) is the Catalan number \(C_{n}\).  
   A standard proof uses the reflection principle:

   *All* words with \(n\) D’s and \(n\) R’s are \(\binom{2n}{n}\).  
   The “bad” words (those that at some point have more D’s than R’s) are in bijection with the words that start with a D and then have \(n-1\) D’s and \(n+1\) R’s; there are \(\binom{2n}{n+1}\) of them.  
   Hence

   \[
   C_{n}= \binom{2n}{n}-\binom{2n}{n+1}
        = \frac{1}{n+1}\binom{2n}{n}.
   \]

---

### Small‑\(n\) check  

| \(n\) | Triangle side | Paths (Catalan) | Illustration |
|------|----------------|----------------|--------------|
| 1    | 1 small triangle | \(C_{1}=1\) | only the single edge |
| 2    | 2 rows          | \(C_{2}=2\) | two distinct monotone routes |
| 3    | 3 rows          | \(C_{3}=5\) | five routes (the classic Dyck‑path picture) |
| 4    | 4 rows          | \(C_{4}=14\) | … |

The numbers match the familiar Catalan sequence \(1,2,5,14,42,\dots\).

---

### Final statement  

Therefore, the number of ways to travel from one corner of a triangular grid of side‑length \(n\) to the opposite corner while never moving upward is exactly the \(n\)-th Catalan number  

\[
\boxed{C_{n}= \frac{1}{n+1}\binom{2n}{n}}.
\]

Can you outline a strategy for this question? An ant walks around a square of insect repellent that is 0.5 meters on each side, always remaining exactly 20 cm away from it. What is the total area enclosed by the ant's path in square centimeters?

We can break it down as follows: The ant’s path is the curve that is everywhere **20 cm** away from the square of side **0.5 m = 50 cm**.  
That curve is the *outer offset* of the square by a distance \(d = 20\) cm.  

For any planar shape, the area of its offset by distance \(d\) is  

\[
\text{Area}_{\text{offset}} = \text{Area}_{\text{original}} + (\text{perimeter})\;d + \pi d^{2}.
\]

---

### 1. Original square  

* Side length: \(s = 50\) cm  
* Area: \(A_{\text{sq}} = s^{2} = 50^{2}=2500\ \text{cm}^{2}\)  
* Perimeter: \(P = 4s = 200\ \text{cm}\)

### 2. Offset distance  

\(d = 20\) cm

### 3. Area of the ant’s path  

\[
\begin{aligned}
A_{\text{path}} &= A_{\text{sq}} + P\,d + \pi d^{2} \\
&= 2500 \;+\; 200\cdot 20 \;+\; \pi\,(20)^{2} \\
&= 2500 \;+\; 4000 \;+\; 400\pi \\
&= 6500 \;+\; 400\pi\ \text{cm}^{2}.
\end{aligned}
\]

---

### 4. Numerical value (optional)

\[
400\pi \approx 400 \times 3.14159 \approx 1256.64,
\]

so  

\[
A_{\text{path}} \approx 6500 + 1256.64 \approx 7756.6\ \text{cm}^{2}.
\]

---

\[
\boxed{A_{\text{path}} = 6500 + 400\pi\ \text{cm}^{2}\ \approx\ 7.76\times10^{3}\ \text{cm}^{2}}
\]

Could you help me make sense of this problem? Using the diagonalization of matrix \( A \), find the fundamental matrix \( \Phi(t) \) with \( \Phi(0) = I \). If \( x_0 = \begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} \), find \( x(t) \) for \( t > 0 \).

First the conclusion, then the reasoning: Below is a **step‑by‑step recipe** that works for **any** \(2\times2\) matrix \(A\) that can be diagonalised.  
All the algebra you have to do for a concrete matrix is collected in the boxed formulas at the end, so you can simply plug‑in the numbers that belong to your particular \(A\).

---

## 1.  Diagonalise \(A\)

1. **Eigenvalues**  
   Solve the characteristic equation  

   \[
   \det(A-\lambda I)=0\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad 
   \lambda_{1},\;\lambda_{2}\in\mathbb C .
   \]

2. **Eigenvectors**  
   For each eigenvalue \(\lambda_i\) find a non‑zero vector \(v_i\) that satisfies  

   \[
   (A-\lambda_i I)v_i=0 .
   \]

3. **Form the modal matrix**  

   \[
   P=\bigl[\,v_{1}\;\;v_{2}\,\bigr]\qquad(\text{columns are the eigenvectors}).
   \]

4. **Construct the diagonal matrix**  

   \[
   D=\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2}) .
   \]

   By construction  

   \[
   A=PDP^{-1}\qquad\text{(the similarity transformation)} .
   \]

---

## 2.  Fundamental matrix \(\Phi(t)\) with \(\Phi(0)=I\)

The matrix exponential of a diagonal matrix is trivial:

\[
e^{Dt}= \operatorname{diag}\bigl(e^{\lambda_{1}t},\,e^{\lambda_{2}t}\bigr).
\]

Hence the **fundamental matrix** (the matrix‑valued solution of \(\dot\Phi=A\Phi\) with \(\Phi(0)=I\)) is

\[
\boxed{\;\Phi(t)=Pe^{Dt}P^{-1}
      =P\begin{bmatrix}
          e^{\lambda_{1}t}&0\\[2pt]
          0&e^{\lambda_{2}t}
        \end{bmatrix}P^{-1}\;}
\tag{1}
\]

Because \(P\) is constant, \(\Phi(0)=PIP^{-1}=I\) automatically.

---

## 3.  State‑trajectory for a given initial condition

Let  

\[
x(0)=x_{0}=\begin{bmatrix}-1\\0\end{bmatrix}.
\]

The solution of the linear system \(\dot x = Ax\) is

\[
x(t)=\Phi(t)x_{0}.
\]

A very convenient way to write the same result is in the **modal (eigen‑mode) form**:

1. Compute the coordinates of the initial vector in the eigen‑basis  

   \[
   c = P^{-1}x_{0}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
   c=\begin{bmatrix}c_{1}\\c_{2}\end{bmatrix}.
   \]

2. Propagate each mode separately  

   \[
   x(t)=c_{1}e^{\lambda_{1}t}v_{1}+c_{2}e^{\lambda_{2}t}v_{2}.
   \tag{2}
   \]

Equation (2) is algebraically identical to (1) but often easier to read.

---

## 4.  **Putting it all together – a concrete example**

Below we illustrate the whole procedure for a typical matrix that appears in textbooks.  
If your matrix \(A\) is different, simply replace the numbers in the boxed formulas.

### Example matrix  

\[
A=\begin{bmatrix}
2 & 1\\[2pt]
1 & 2
\end{bmatrix}.
\]

#### (a) Eigen‑values  

\[
\det\!\begin{pmatrix}2-\lambda & 1\\ 1 & 2-\lambda\end{pmatrix}
=(2-\lambda)^{2}-1=0
\;\Longrightarrow\;
\lambda_{1}=3,\qquad \lambda_{2}=1 .
\]

#### (b) Eigen‑vectors  

* For \(\lambda_{1}=3\): \((A-3I)v=0\Rightarrow\begin{bmatrix}-1&1\\1&-1\end{bmatrix}v=0\)
  gives \(v_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}1\\1\end{bmatrix}\).

* For \(\lambda_{2}=1\): \((A- I)v=0\Rightarrow\begin{bmatrix}1&1\\1&1\end{bmatrix}v=0\)
  gives \(v_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}1\\-1\end{bmatrix}\).

#### (c) Matrices \(P\) and \(D\)

\[
P=\begin{bmatrix}1&1\\[2pt]1&-1\end{bmatrix},
\qquad
D=\begin{bmatrix}3&0\\0&1\end{bmatrix},
\qquad
P^{-1}= \frac12\begin{bmatrix}1&1\\[2pt]1&-1\end{bmatrix}.
\]

#### (d) Fundamental matrix  

\[
\Phi(t)=P\begin{bmatrix}e^{3t}&0\\0&e^{t}\end{bmatrix}P^{-1}
      =\frac12\begin{bmatrix}
          e^{3t}+e^{t} & e^{3t}-e^{t}\\[4pt]
          e^{3t}-e^{t} & e^{3t}+e^{t}
        \end{bmatrix}.
\]

One can verify that \(\Phi(0)=I\).

#### (e) Trajectory for \(x_{0}=(-1,0)^{\!T}\)

* Coordinates in the eigen‑basis  

  \[
  c=P^{-1}x_{0}
    =\frac12\begin{bmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{bmatrix}
      \begin{bmatrix}-1\\0\end{bmatrix}
    =\begin{bmatrix}-\tfrac12\\-\tfrac12\end{bmatrix}.
  \]

* Modal solution (2)  

  \[
  x(t)=c_{1}e^{3t}v_{1}+c_{2}e^{t}v_{2}
       =-\frac12e^{3t}\begin{bmatrix}1\\1\end{bmatrix}
        -\frac12e^{t}\begin{bmatrix}1\\-1\end{bmatrix}
       =\frac12\begin{bmatrix}
                -e^{3t}-e^{t}\\[2pt]
                -e^{3t}+e^{t}
               \end{bmatrix}.
  \]

Equivalently, using \(\Phi(t)\),

\[
x(t)=\Phi(t)x_{0}
     =\frac12\begin{bmatrix}
               -(e^{3t}+e^{t})\\[2pt]
               -(e^{3t}-e^{t})
              \end{bmatrix},
\qquad t>0 .
\]

---

## 5.  Summary – **What you need to do for your own \(A\)**  

1. **Find eigenvalues \(\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2}\).**  
2. **Find corresponding eigenvectors \(v_{1},v_{2}\).**  
3. **Form** \(P=[v_{1}\;v_{2}]\) **and** \(D=\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2})\).  
4. **Write the fundamental matrix**  

   \[
   \boxed{\Phi(t)=P\begin{bmatrix}e^{\lambda_{1}t}&0\\0&e^{\lambda_{2}t}\end{bmatrix}P^{-1}}.
   \]

5. **Compute** \(c=P^{-1}x_{0}\) **and then**  

   \[
   \boxed{x(t)=c_{1}e^{\lambda_{1}t}v_{1}+c_{2}e^{\lambda_{2}t}v_{2}
          =\Phi(t)x_{0}}.
   \]

That gives you the unique solution of the linear system \(\dot x=Ax\) satisfying the initial condition \(x(0)=x_{0}\) for all \(t>0\).

I tried a few ideas but failed. What's the right approach? Solve the equation $x^{2}+y^{3} = z^{4}$ where $x, y,$ and $z$ are positive integers, but $y$ is not prime.

Alright, here's a step-by-step explanation: \[
x^{2}+y^{3}=z^{4},\qquad x,y,z\in \mathbb Z_{>0},\;y\hbox{ composite}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  A convenient factorisation  

Put  

\[
a=z^{2}\qquad (a>0)
\]

so that the equation becomes  

\[
a^{2}-x^{2}=y^{3}\Longrightarrow (a-x)(a+x)=y^{3}. \tag{1}
\]

Denote  

\[
u=a-x,\qquad v=a+x .
\]

Then  

\[
u\,v=y^{3},\qquad u<v,\qquad u\equiv v\pmod 2      \tag{2}
\]

(the parity condition follows from \(u+v=2a\) being even).  
Conversely, if a pair \((u,v)\) satisfies (2) we obtain  

\[
a=\frac{u+v}{2},\qquad x=\frac{v-u}{2},\qquad z^{2}=a .
\]

Hence we have to find a factor‑pair \((u,v)\) of the perfect cube \(y^{3}\) such that  

\[
\frac{u+v}{2}\ \text{is a perfect square}. \tag{3}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Writing the factors as cubes  

Write  

\[
u=d^{3},\qquad v=k^{3},
\]

where \(d,k\) are positive integers with \(d\mid y\) and \(k=\dfrac{y}{d}\) (so that
\(d\,k=y\)).  
Equation (3) becomes  

\[
\frac{d^{3}+k^{3}}{2}=z^{2}. \tag{4}
\]

Thus we need two positive integers \(d,k\) with  

\[
d^{3}+k^{3}=2z^{2}. \tag{5}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Solving \(d^{3}+k^{3}=2z^{2}\)

Put \(k=m\,d\;(m>1)\).  Then (5) reads  

\[
d^{3}\bigl(1+m^{3}\bigr)=2z^{2}. \tag{6}
\]

Factor \(1+m^{3}\) as  

\[
1+m^{3}=2\,s^{2}\,c ,\qquad s,c\in\mathbb Z_{>0}. \tag{7}
\]

(For every integer \(m\) the right‑hand side can be achieved by taking  
\(s=\sqrt{\dfrac{1+m^{3}}{2c}}\); we shall use the values of \(m\) for which
\(1+m^{3}\) is even, i.e. \(m\) odd.)

Now choose  

\[
d=s\,c\,t^{2}\qquad(t\in\mathbb Z_{>0}). \tag{8}
\]

Then from (6)–(8)

\[
z^{2}= \bigl(s^{2}c^{2}t^{3}\bigr)^{2},\qquad 
z=s^{2}c^{2}t^{3}. \tag{9}
\]

Consequently

\[
\boxed{\;
\begin{aligned}
d &= s\,c\,t^{2},\\[2mm]
k &= m\,d = m\,s\,c\,t^{2},\\[2mm]
y &= d\,k = m\,s^{2}c^{2}t^{4},\\[2mm]
a &=\frac{d^{3}+k^{3}}{2}=z^{2}=s^{4}c^{4}t^{6},\\[2mm]
z &= s^{2}c^{2}t^{3},\\[2mm]
x &=\frac{k^{3}-d^{3}}{2}= \frac{m^{3}-1}{2}\,s^{3}c^{3}t^{6}.
\end{aligned}
\;}
\tag{10}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4.  The smallest odd value of \(m\)

The simplest choice is \(m=2\) (the smallest odd \(m\) that makes
\(1+m^{3}=9\) a perfect square).  
For \(m=2\) we have  

\[
1+m^{3}=9=3^{2}\cdot 1 =2\cdot 3^{2}\cdot\frac12 .
\]

Taking \(s=3,\;c=1\) in (7) gives  

\[
d=2t^{2},\qquad k=4t^{2}.
\]

Substituting these values into (10) yields the **parametric family**

\[
\boxed{\;
\begin{aligned}
x &= 28\,t^{6},\\
y &= 8\,t^{4},\\
z &= 6\,t^{3},
\end{aligned}\qquad t\in\mathbb Z_{>0}.}
\tag{11}
\]

Every triple \((x,y,z)\) given by (11) satisfies  

\[
x^{2}+y^{3}=z^{4},
\]

and \(y=8t^{4}\) is never prime (it is a multiple of \(8\)).  
For \(t=1\) we obtain the smallest solution  

\[
(x,y,z)=(28,\,8,\,6),
\]

and for \(t=2\),

\[
(x,y,z)=(28\cdot 2^{6},\,8\cdot 2^{4},\,6\cdot 2^{3})=(1792,\,128,\,48),
\]

etc.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 5.  No other solutions with \(y\) composite

Equation (1) forces the two factors of \(y^{3}\) to be perfect cubes,
otherwise \(\frac{u+v}{2}\) could not be a square.
Hence every solution must arise from a pair of cubes \((d^{3},k^{3})\) with
\(d\,k=y\) and must satisfy (5).  
The analysis above shows that (5) is equivalent to (6); the only way to
make the left–hand side a twice‑square is to write \(1+m^{3}=2s^{2}c\) and
to take \(d=s\,c\,t^{2}\).  This produces exactly the family (10).  
Choosing any other odd \(m\) gives a different family, but all of them are
contained in (10).  The smallest odd \(m\) is \(m=2\), which yields the
simplest and most compact description (11).  

Thus **all** positive‑integer solutions with composite \(y\) are given by
(11); in particular the smallest one is \((28,8,6)\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 6.  Answer  

\[
\boxed{\;(x,y,z)=\bigl(28\,t^{6},\;8\,t^{4},\;6\,t^{3}\bigr)\qquad
(t=1,2,3,\dots)\;}
\]

Every triple of this form satisfies \(x^{2}+y^{3}=z^{4}\) and has
\(y\) composite; conversely, any solution with \(y\) composite is of this
form.  The first solution is \((x,y,z)=(28,8,6)\).
I'm stuck on this problem—could you help? Solve the given inequalities: $|x+1|+|x-2|>5$.

Alright, here's a step-by-step explanation: \[
|x+1|+|x-2|>5
\]

The absolute‑value expression changes its form at the points where the arguments are zero, i.e. at  

\[
x=-1\qquad\text{and}\qquad x=2 .
\]

Hence we examine three intervals.

---

### 1.  \(x\le -1\)

\[
\begin{aligned}
|x+1| &= -(x+1) = -x-1,\\
|x-2| &= -(x-2) = -x+2.
\end{aligned}
\]

Thus  

\[
|x+1|+|x-2| = (-x-1)+(-x+2)= -2x+1 .
\]

The inequality becomes  

\[
-2x+1>5\quad\Longrightarrow\quad -2x>4\quad\Longrightarrow\quad x<-2 .
\]

Intersecting with the interval \(x\le -1\) gives  

\[
(-\infty,-2).
\]

---

### 2.  \(-1\le x\le 2\)

Here  

\[
|x+1| = x+1,\qquad |x-2| = -(x-2) = -x+2,
\]

so  

\[
|x+1|+|x-2| = (x+1)+(-x+2)=3 .
\]

Since \(3>5\) is false, **no** \(x\) in \([-1,2]\) satisfies the inequality.

---

### 3.  \(x\ge 2\)

Now both arguments are non‑negative:

\[
|x+1| = x+1,\qquad |x-2| = x-2,
\]

hence  

\[
|x+1|+|x-2| = (x+1)+(x-2)=2x-1 .
\]

The inequality becomes  

\[
2x-1>5\quad\Longrightarrow\quad 2x>6\quad\Longrightarrow\quad x>3 .
\]

Intersecting with \(x\ge 2\) yields  

\[
(3,\infty).
\]

---

### Solution set

Combining the admissible intervals:

\[
\boxed{\,(-\infty,-2)\ \cup\ (3,\infty)\,}.
\]

(Endpoints \(-2\) and \(3\) give equality \(=5\), not a strict “greater than”, so they are excluded.)
What would be a clean way to solve this? Find the maximum possible integer \( n \) such that \(\frac{(n - 1)(n^2 + n - 3)}{n^2 + 4}\) is also an integer.

We can break it down as follows: \[
\frac{(n-1)(n^{2}+n-3)}{n^{2}+4}
   =\frac{n^{3}-4n+3}{n^{2}+4}
\]

Let  

\[
k=\frac{n^{3}-4n+3}{n^{2}+4}\in\mathbb Z .
\]

The condition “\(k\) is an integer’’ is equivalent to  

\[
n^{2}+4\mid n^{3}-4n+3 .
\]

---

### 1. Reduce the numerator modulo the denominator  

Since \(n^{2}\equiv -4\pmod{n^{2}+4}\),

\[
n^{3}=n\cdot n^{2}\equiv n(-4)=-4n\pmod{n^{2}+4}.
\]

Hence  

\[
n^{3}-4n+3\equiv -4n-4n+3=-8n+3\pmod{n^{2}+4}.
\]

Thus  

\[
n^{2}+4\mid -8n+3\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad n^{2}+4\mid 8n-3 .
\]

---

### 2. Bounding possible \(n\)

For \(|n|\ge 8\),

\[
|8n-3|<n^{2}+4,
\]

so the only way the divisibility can hold is \(8n-3=0\), i.e. \(n=\frac38\), which is not an integer.  
Therefore any integer solution must satisfy \(|n|\le 7\).

---

### 3. Test the remaining integers  

We only need to check \(n=-7,-6,\dots ,7\).

\mathbf{7}  & 318  & 53 & \mathbf{6}\in\mathbb Z
\end{array}
\]

Only \(n=1\) and \(n=7\) make the fraction an integer.

---

### 4. Maximum integer \(n\)

The largest integer among the solutions is

Where should I start to avoid common pitfalls? Find the volume of a regular quadrangular pyramid the side of whose base is $a$ and the dihedral angle between the lateral faces is $\alpha $.

Here's a clear solution: Let  

* the square base have side \(a\);
* the centre of the base be the origin \(O(0,0,0)\);
* the apex be \(S(0,0,h)\) (the pyramid is regular, therefore the apex is above the centre);
* the vertices of the base be  

\[
A\Bigl(\frac a2,\frac a2,0\Bigr),\;
B\Bigl(-\frac a2,\frac a2,0\Bigr),\;
C\Bigl(-\frac a2,-\frac a2,0\Bigr),\;
D\Bigl(\frac a2,-\frac a2,0\Bigr).
\]

The two lateral faces that meet along the lateral edge \(SB\) are the triangles
\(SAB\) and \(SBC\).  
The dihedral angle between these faces is the given \(\alpha\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  Express \(\alpha\) through the height \(h\)

Vectors belonging to the two faces are  

\[
\vec{SA}= \Bigl(\frac a2,\frac a2,-h\Bigr),\qquad
\vec{SB}= \Bigl(-\frac a2,\frac a2,-h\Bigr),\qquad
\vec{SC}= \Bigl(-\frac a2,-\frac a2,-h\Bigr).
\]

Normals to the faces are

\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf n_1 &= \vec{SA}\times\vec{SB}
            =\bigl(0,\;ah,\; \tfrac{a^{2}}{2}\bigr),\\[2mm]
\mathbf n_2 &= \vec{SB}\times\vec{SC}
            =\bigl(-ah,\;0,\; \tfrac{a^{2}}{2}\bigr).
\end{aligned}
\]

The dihedral angle \(\alpha\) equals the angle between the normals:

\[
\cos\alpha=\frac{\mathbf n_1\!\cdot\!\mathbf n_2}
                 {\|\mathbf n_1\|\,\|\mathbf n_2\|}
          =\frac{a^{4}/4}{a^{2}\bigl(h^{2}+a^{2}/4\bigr)}
          =\frac{a^{2}}{4h^{2}+a^{2}} .
\]

Hence  

\[
4h^{2}+a^{2}= \frac{a^{2}}{\cos\alpha}
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
h^{2}= \frac{a^{2}}{4}\,\frac{1-\cos\alpha}{\cos\alpha}.
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Height of the pyramid

\[
\boxed{\,h=\frac{a}{2}\sqrt{\frac{1-\cos\alpha}{\cos\alpha}}\,}.
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Volume

The volume of a pyramid is \(\displaystyle V=\frac13\;(\text{area of base})\times(\text{height})\).

The base area is \(a^{2}\); therefore

\[
\begin{aligned}
V&=\frac13 a^{2}h
   =\frac13 a^{2}\,\frac{a}{2}
      \sqrt{\frac{1-\cos\alpha}{\cos\alpha}}\\[2mm]
  &=\boxed{\displaystyle
     \frac{a^{3}}{6}\sqrt{\frac{1-\cos\alpha}{\cos\alpha}} }.
\end{aligned}
\]

Using the half‑angle identity \(1-\cos\alpha=2\sin^{2}\frac{\alpha}{2}\) one may also write

\[
\boxed{ \displaystyle
V=\frac{a^{3}}{3\sqrt{2}}\,
   \frac{\sin\frac{\alpha}{2}}{\sqrt{\cos\alpha}} } .
\]

Both formulas give the volume of a regular quadrangular (square‑based) pyramid in terms of the side length \(a\) of the base and the dihedral angle \(\alpha\) between two adjacent lateral faces.
Where should I start to avoid common pitfalls? How many sequences of seven lights, each of which can be red, blue, or green, are there such that all three colors are used at least once?

Here's the core idea and its execution: We have a string of length \(7\) where each position can be colored **red (R)**, **blue (B)**, or **green (G)**.  
We want the number of such strings that contain **all three colors at least once**.

---

### 1. Count all possible strings  

Without any restriction each of the 7 positions can be any of the 3 colors:

\[
\text{Total}=3^{7}=2187 .
\]

---

### 2. Exclude strings that miss at least one color  

Use the Inclusion–Exclusion Principle.

* **Missing a specific color**  
  Choose the color that does **not** appear (3 choices).  
  The remaining 7 positions can then be filled with only the other two colors, giving \(2^{7}\) strings.

  \[
  \text{Count}_{1}=3\cdot 2^{7}=3\cdot128=384 .
  \]

* **Missing two colors (i.e., using only one color)**  
  Choose the single color that is used (3 choices).  
  All 7 positions must be that color, giving \(1^{7}=1\) string for each choice.

  \[
  \text{Count}_{2}=3\cdot 1=3 .
  \]

There is no way to miss all three colors, so the inclusion–exclusion formula stops here.

---

### 3. Apply Inclusion–Exclusion  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{Desired number}
&= \text{Total}
   - \text{Count}_{1}
   + \text{Count}_{2} \\
&= 3^{7} - 3\cdot 2^{7} + 3 \\
&= 2187 - 384 + 3 \\
&= 1806 .
\end{aligned}
\]

---

\[
\boxed{1806}
\]

Starting from basics, how should I solve this? Given a derivable function \( f: \mathbb{R} \setminus \{0\} \to \mathbb{R} \) that satisfies \( f(x^2 + y^2) = f(2xy) + f(x^2 - y^2) \) for all \( x, y \in \mathbb{R} \) and \( f(1) = 2 \), find \( f(3) + f(4) \).

First the conclusion, then the reasoning: \[
f:\mathbb R\setminus\{0\}\longrightarrow\mathbb R ,\qquad 
f(x^{2}+y^{2})=f(2xy)+f(x^{2}-y^{2})\qquad(\forall x,y\in\mathbb R)
\tag{1}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  Re‑writing the equation  

Put  

\[
a=x^{2}-y^{2},\qquad b=2xy .
\]

Then  

\[
a^{2}+b^{2}=(x^{2}-y^{2})^{2}+(2xy)^{2}=(x^{2}+y^{2})^{2},
\qquad 
x^{2}+y^{2}= \sqrt{a^{2}+b^{2}}\;(>0).
\]

Conversely, for any real numbers \(a,b\) (not both zero) there exist
real \(x,y\) such that \(a=x^{2}-y^{2},\;b=2xy\) (they are the real and
imaginary parts of a square root of the complex number \(a+ib\)).
Hence (1) is equivalent to  

\[
\boxed{\,f\!\bigl(\sqrt{a^{2}+b^{2}}\bigr)=f(a)+f(b)}\qquad
(\forall a,b\neq 0). \tag{2}
\]

Thus the value of \(f\) at the length of the hypotenuse of a right
triangle equals the sum of the values at the two legs.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Homogeneity  

Take \(b=a\neq0\) in (2).  Since \(\sqrt{a^{2}+a^{2}}=\sqrt{2}\,|a|\),

\[
f\bigl(\sqrt{2}\,|a|\bigr)=2f(a)\qquad(\forall a\neq0). \tag{3}
\]

Replacing \(a\) by \(\lambda a\) (\(\lambda>0\)) and using (3) repeatedly
gives  

\[
f(\lambda a)=\lambda^{2}f(a)\qquad(\forall a\neq0,\;\lambda>0). \tag{4}
\]

Because \(f\) is differentiable (hence continuous), (4) extends from
\(\lambda=\sqrt{2}^{\,n}\;(n\in\mathbb Z)\) to **every** positive real
\(\lambda\).  Consequently  

\[
f(\lambda t)=\lambda^{2}f(t)\qquad(\forall t\neq0,\;\lambda>0). \tag{5}
\]

In particular, for \(t>0\) we have \(f(t)=t^{2}f(1)\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Determination of the constant  

From the hypothesis \(f(1)=2\),

\[
f(t)=2t^{2}\qquad(\forall t>0). \tag{6}
\]

For a negative argument \(t<0\) we use (2) with \(a=t,\;b=0\) is not
allowed (the term \(f(0)\) is undefined), but we can write \(t=-u\) with
\(u>0\) and choose \(a=u,\;b=0\) after a sign change in the original
variables; the homogeneity (5) gives the same formula for negative
\(t\).  Hence (6) holds for **all** \(t\neq0\):

\[
\boxed{\,f(t)=2t^{2}\qquad(t\in\mathbb R\setminus\{0\})\,}.
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4.  Computing \(f(3)+f(4)\)

\[
f(3)=2\cdot3^{2}=18,\qquad 
f(4)=2\cdot4^{2}=32,
\]

\[
\boxed{f(3)+f(4)=18+32=50}.
\]
